title_original: Interview: Lynne Ramsay on Die My Love
editorial_title_zh: 访谈：琳恩·拉姆塞谈《Die My Love》
editorial_excerpt_zh: 超越自我：这位苏格兰作者导演谈论她的最新力作，一如既往地精准刻画了一个深不可测的角色
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在苏格兰导演琳恩·拉姆塞（Lynne Ramsay）的最新长片——她自2017年的《你从未在此》以来的首部作品中，她的镜头再次对准了一个难以捉摸的角色、一个社会边缘人，一个既因不愿墨守成规而令人钦佩、又同样让人感到刺痛的人物。影片改编自阿根廷作家阿里安娜·哈维奇（Ariana Harwicz）的小说，《Die My Love》由詹妮弗·劳伦斯（Jennifer Lawrence）和罗伯特·帕丁森（Robert Pattinson）主演，饰演一对刚从纽约搬到丈夫位于蒙大拿州乡村老家的年轻夫妇。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "空气又厚又湿，破败的房子既宏大又孤寂，而在电影开场不久便生下孩子的格蕾丝（劳伦斯饰）开始崩溃：要做的事实在太多，却又无所事事，随着母职的责任将她压垮，她开始陷入孤立与产后抑郁的泥潭。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "拉姆塞以其一贯精准、富有诗意的视觉和声音设计将小说搬上银幕，塑造出一部某种意义上的当代哥特式情节剧。劳伦斯以带有克制歇斯底里的表演为影片定下基调，而帕丁森、西茜·斯派塞克（饰演格蕾丝的婆婆）以及勒凯斯·斯坦菲尔德（饰演成为格蕾丝执念对象的邻居）则通过配角表演增添了细微差别与质感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Die My Love》目前正在院线热映。在今年的戛纳电影节首映后，我与拉姆塞坐下来，就这部电影的创作进行了交谈。就在电影节开幕前几天，她刚失去了母亲，悲伤给见证观众发现这部电影的喜悦蒙上了一层阴影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对你母亲的离去表示哀悼。我确信在这一切之中还要做这些一定很难。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的，因为我本来打算邀请她来这儿。不过没关系。我现在已经释怀了。她活了很长时间。她80岁了。但她头脑清醒，而且很幽默。这总是很难的。那是你的妈妈，你知道的吧？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当然。而且你的电影总是关于孩子和母亲的。这一定是一次挺奇妙的精神体验。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的[笑]。但从某种程度上说，这也挺好，因为我没有把这看得太严肃。我想我第一次来这儿的时候还很年轻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "带着你的毕业短片《微小死亡》（1996），对吧？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对。我当时真的很紧张。现在我感觉放松多了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是你第八次来到戛纳。没有多少人能来过八次。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我感觉自己更清楚流程是怎么回事了。我记得带着《凯恩怎么了》（2011）来这里的时候，我超级紧张。我丈夫是个音乐家，我把他的手抓得那么紧，差点把他的手指捏断。他说：“那可是我弹吉他的手！”[笑]但这一次，我感觉相当放松。我很喜欢这部电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我是在来这里的航班上读完这部电影所改编的阿里安娜·哈维奇的小说的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "那是一本很难读、很难啃的小说——因为它在时间上跳跃，而且相当黑暗。我其实不想走那条路。我改变了它，扭转了它。我不想再拍一部《凯恩》那种风格的东西。老实说，那让我有点打退堂鼓。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不知道自己是不是从看完《凯恩怎么了》之后缓过劲来了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我知道。说来也巧，那时我还没有孩子，但现在我有了。每当有母亲走过来对我说“我们看过《凯恩》了”，我就会说：“我很抱歉！”我对《Die My Love》的看法是，我想在其中加入一些幽默，并吸收小说中的一些想法和主题——那种动物般的感觉、格蕾丝的性本能——但把它拍成一个爱情故事。一个疯狂的、歇斯底里的爱情故事，而不是一个产后故事。当人们说“产后”时，我会说：“那不是一部产后电影。”它既是也不是。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我很想听听你是如何将小说中的内心独白转化为一部让我们保持一定距离的电影的。你以前合作过许多采用第一人称讲述的小说，并且对它们做了非常有趣的处理。对于《Die My Love》，另一个电影人可能会选择走捷径使用画外音。但你却从这个长镜头、疏离且静态的房屋全景开始；你从未让我们完全窥探女主角的内心世界。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我想这是因为我最初是个画家，然后是一名摄影师。事实上，我还想再次成为一名画家；那是我的志向。我更多地是用画面而不是文字思考。作为一名电影人，这非常方便。我会构想一个关键意象。在这里，最初的事情是，他们搬进了这座新房子，也许他们以前住在纽约。这是我的背景故事：他曾是一名音乐家。她写过几篇发表过的作品。房子是免费的，但它却在鸟不生蛋的鬼地方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "常规做法是从外部拍摄这座房子。而我想，不，我要从房子“看着他们”的视角来拍。我会让他们走进房子，然后我们用一个固定镜头。所以这算是一种关键意象。几乎就像房子本身是活的一样。然后你会听到老鼠的声音，带有一点不祥的预感。但其中也存在希望。丈夫在说——我们要这么做。楼上有专门给你的办公室。我会把我的架子鼓搬来。我们可以在这里做任何我们想做的事。所以在一切开始分崩离析之前，这里其实是充满希望的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你刚才说你想把它拍成一个爱情故事。我很受触动的一点是，你并没有为格蕾丝的精神失常和悲伤辩护，也没有把任何人塑造为反派。她的丈夫在尽力做到最好。很多类似的故事都会把婆婆刻薄化，但在这里，她也是富有同情心的。就像你说的，房子里有希望存在。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "嗯，我觉得相比于设定那些类型化的角色——比如恶母或者那种对她施暴的丈夫——去展现他们之间存在真实的爱，要有趣得多。但这里面存在着误解。她有点像一头野兽。她不按常理出牌，几乎是个无政府主义者，你知道吗？由于感到沮丧，她仿佛在把整个世界砸个稀烂。但我不想用这些简单的答案去给它合理化。我觉得她就是厌烦了；她遇上了写作瓶颈；她和丈夫在一段时间里处于不同的世界。她刚生完孩子，生活开始有一点点分崩离析。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你所有的电影最让我喜欢的一点，就是你确实让我们直面了一种不可知性。哪怕在《凯文怎么了》和《莫文·卡勒》（2002）中，你也没有去解释人。人性中存在着一个不可知的核心，而你让我们真正去审视这一点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是我着迷的东西。《莫文·卡勒》属于那种神秘的类型。你永远不知道她在想什么。原著小说里全都是独白，全是在解释她的想法。但我没有用旁白。即使在小说里，她也是个高深莫测的角色。所以我认为她应该保持这种神秘，就像西部片里那些骑马消失在夕阳中的牛仔一样。我和我最好的朋友之一[莉安娜·多尼尼]共同编剧了那部电影，她不幸英年早逝。但我们一直觉得莫文就像个牛仔。而在这里，我看到的是一个无政府主义者。我看到的是一个要将世界付之一炬的人。而且我觉得她在她的男孩身上看到了自己的倒影，这太可怕了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部小说故事发生在法国。原著作者阿里安娜·哈维奇是阿根廷人……", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在这里见到了她，她太棒了。她真的很喜欢这部电影。来这之前我从没见过她。我当时有点像：“天哪，感觉我把你的书给毁了。”但实际上，我觉得她看出我捕捉到了它的精髓，尽管形式有所不同。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "太棒了！决定将背景设在美国是你的决定，还是在你加入项目之前就定好的？因为这本书极具地方特色，深深植根于法国乡村那种特定的环境与生活，而电影感觉非常美国化。它浸润在蒙大拿州乡村的风光、口音和气候之中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是我的决定。我觉得美国就像是由不同的国家组成的。你去了纽约，再去蒙大拿，那完全是截然不同的情况。如果你住在纽约，然后搬到了穷乡僻壤，比方说，那是一个巨大的转变。在美国流离失所……你知道的，很多人搬家是因为他们没有足够的钱，无法继续留在纽约，诸如此类。角色们得到了这栋免费的房子，所以他们就接受了。但随后她就想：“这特么是什么鬼？我在荒郊野岭。我其实什么也没有。”大概帕姆——也就是婆婆——才是最能看穿她的人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在你为标准收藏（Criterion Collection）做的一篇采访里读到，你母亲过去常看道格拉斯·瑟克和希区柯克的 melodrama。詹妮弗·劳伦斯的这个角色身上，确实有些地方让我想起经典 melodrama 的女主角。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我很喜欢那种电影。道格拉斯·瑟克其实相当大胆，因为他拍的是以女性为主角的故事。而且你知道吗，他也拍了大量涉及禁忌的内容。老实说，我从那种电影中汲取了很多灵感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她的一头金发、刘海，还有微微嘟起的嘴唇，就是有某种特质让我想起那些女主角。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你知道的，我们在刘海上花了很长时间。起初詹妮弗说：“我不想留刘海。”我说：“我希望你留刘海。你看起来会更害羞一点。”当时我想：“哦，她大概要抓狂了。”但她并没有。她说：“我很喜欢。我很喜欢。”她一直保留着这个发型。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这就是你眼中的她？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对，维罗妮卡·莱克。你知道吧？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在同一篇标准收藏的采访中，采访者提到了另一个让我印象深刻的细节：你的很多电影里都有这样一个镜头——角色把蕾丝窗帘裹在头上。这次在这里又出现了。这是怎么回事？这难道就是林恩·拉姆西内心的钥匙吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "嗯，这纯粹是巧合，当我去做堪景时，我走上楼，那里刚好挂着一张那样漂亮的窗帘。我也不知道为什么。也许只是对《捕鼠者》（1999）的一点致敬。但这是我写下的第一个意象。它是一个小主题。我觉得它有点像是一件寿衣，你知道吗？而且它也带着一丝光亮。我的意思是，在《捕鼠者》里有一种顽皮感，随后它变得黑暗起来。至于格蕾丝，她身处这个地方内部，某种程度上被困住了。所以就像被关在玻璃罩里一样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我对拉凯斯·斯坦菲尔德的角色很感兴趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他太棒了。实际上我很想拍一部以他为主角的电影。但这只是个很小的角色，对他来说能演这个很棒。我想他真的很喜欢这个剧本，并且想参与其中。而且这个角色在书里也是——他是真的还是假的？这是我想玩味的东西。当格蕾丝在停车场看到他们时，那种感觉就像是：“哦天哪，他是真的，他有家庭，他有孩子。”现实很残酷。人们在外界都有自己的生活。拉凯斯有着如此强大的存在感，哪怕戏份很少，他也确实留下了深刻的印记。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我觉得很有意思的是，在这个中产阶级白人女性封闭世界的边缘，竟然有这样一个黑人男性和黑人家庭。种族一直是那些经典 melodrama 的一部分，即便没有被明说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我觉得（这个角色）是黑人还是白人都行，但我挺喜欢这样的。因为他们有更好的房子。比如，是格蕾丝和杰克逊（帕斯汀饰演的角色）住着破烂的房子。拉凯斯的角色大概从事建筑之类的工作，像是个知识分子。我是这么看的。当你看到拉凯斯居住的那栋房子的镜头时，那是一栋非常漂亮的房子。这只是被巧妙地暗示了而已。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "电影里的那些歌曲构成了另一种剧本。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "嗯，我想在我的背景设定里，他是个失败的音乐人，所以他会有一大堆唱片收藏。我想你会在某个镜头里看到它。然后我想，当她感到无聊时，她就会一遍又一遍地播放同样的唱片，比如[托妮·贝塞尔（Toni Basil）录制的]《米奇》（“Mickey”）。此外，在拍这部电影之前，我曾和荒野乐队（the Bad Seeds）的吉他手乔治[·维杰斯蒂卡（George Vjestica）]合作过。我写了很多歌，因为我厌倦了等待电影开拍。我想，我要写歌——至少它们很即兴，就像宝丽来相片一样。乔治来到我的公寓，我开始唱这首歌，他开始弹奏。咔嚓！就这样成了。我们大概在半小时内写了三首歌。然后他邀请我去录音室。我开始唱一首叫《零》（“Zero”）的歌，完全是即兴发挥。这就是电影开头的朋克音乐曲目的由来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然后我当时在放《爱会将我们撕裂》（“Love Will Tear Us Apart”），本片的音乐总监雷夫·伯切尔（Raife Burchell）叫我试着唱唱看。我们在乡下，我只是用 iPhone 录了下来，然后他进行了混音。我很讨厌自己的声音，所以我想改变它，但每个人都说：“这太棒了”——他们说服我用了它[作为片尾曲]。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Scottish director Lynne Ramsay’s latest feature—her first since 2017’s You Were Never Really Here —she turns her lens once again on an inscrutable character, a misfit in society, someone as admirable in her unwillingness to abide by the rules as she is abrasive. Adapted from a novel by Argentine author Ariana Harwicz, Die My Love stars Jennifer Lawrence and Robert Pattinson as a young couple who’ve just moved from New York to a house in the husband’s rural Montana hometown."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The air is thick and humid, the decrepit house is big and lonely, and Grace (Lawrence), who gives birth early on in the movie, starts to unravel: there’s both too much to do and too little, and she begins to sink into the quagmire of isolation and postpartum depression as responsibilities of motherhood weigh her down."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ramsay brings the novel to life with a typically precise, poetic visual and sound design, crafting something of a modern-day Gothic melodrama. Lawrence anchors the film with a performance of controlled hysteria, while Pattinson, Sissy Spacek (who plays Grace’s mother-in-law), and LaKeith Stanfield (as a neighbor who becomes an object of Grace’s fixation) add nuance and texture in supporting roles."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die My Love is currently playing in theaters. After its premiere at this year’s Cannes Film Festival, I sat down with Ramsay for a chat about its making. She had just lost her mother days before the festival, and grief tinged her thrill at seeing audiences discover the movie."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My condolences about your mother. I’m sure this must be hard to do in the midst of all that."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah, ’cause I was going to invite her here. But it’s okay. I’m at peace with it now. She lived a long life. She was 80. But she had a good mind, and she was funny. It’s always hard. Your mom, you know?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Of course. And your films are about children and mothers. This must be a bit of a head trip."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah [ laughs ]. But in a way, it’s kind of good, because I’m not taking this too seriously. I think the first time I came here I was quite young."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "With your graduate short film, Small Deaths (1996), right?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah. I was really nervous. Now I feel a bit more relaxed."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This is your eighth time at Cannes. Not many people have been here eight times."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I feel a bit more like I know the drill. I remember when I came here with We Need to Talk About Kevin (2011), I was super nervous. My husband is a musician, and I held his hand so tight I nearly broke his fingers. He was like, “That’s my guitar hand!” [ laughs ] But this time, I feel quite relaxed. I like the film."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I read the novel by Ariana Harwicz, which the film is based on, on the flight here."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s a hard novel to read—to get through—because it jumps through time, and it’s quite dark as well. I didn’t really want to go that way. I changed that, skewered it. I didn’t want to do another Kevin kind of thing. That put me off, to be honest."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I don’t know if I’ve ever recovered from watching We Need to Talk About Kevin ."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I know. Funnily enough, I hadn’t had any children then, but now I do. Every time a mother comes up and says, “We watched Kevin ,” I’m like, “I’m sorry!” The way I looked at Die My Love is I wanted to put some humor in there, and I wanted to take some of the ideas, the themes of the novel—the animalistic kind of feeling, the sexual nature of Grace—but make it a love story. A bonkers, crazy love story, rather than a postpartum story. When people say “postpartum,” I’m like, “That’s not a postpartum movie.” It is and it isn’t."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I’d love to hear about how you translated the inner monologue of the novel into a film that keeps us at arm’s length. You’ve worked before with many novels that are told in the first person, and done very interesting things with them. With Die My Love , another filmmaker might have taken the easy route and done voiceover. But you start with this long, remote, static shot of the house; you never give us full access to the heroine’s mind."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I suppose it’s ’cause I started as a painter, and then a photographer. I’d like to be a painter again, actually; that’s my ambition. I think more in pictures than words. And that’s really handy as a filmmaker. I think of a key image. Here, the first thing was, they’re moving into this new house, and maybe they’ve lived in New York before. This is my backstory: he’s been a musician. She’s written a couple of things that got published. The house is free, but it’s in the bloody middle of nowhere."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The conventional thing to do is to shoot the house from outside. And I thought, no, I’ll shoot the house looking at them . And I’ll have them coming into the house, and we’ll do a locked-off shot. So that’s a sort of key image. It’s almost like the house is alive itself. Then you hear the rats, and there’s something a little bit ominous. But there’s hope in it, as well. The husband is saying—we’re going to do this. article_text:
In Scottish director Lynne Ramsay’s latest feature—her first since 2017’s You Were Never Really Here —she turns her lens once again on an inscrutable character, a misfit in society, someone as admirable in her unwillingness to abide by the rules as she is abrasive. Adapted from a novel by Argentine author Ariana Harwicz, Die My Love stars Jennifer Lawrence and Robert Pattinson as a young couple who’ve just moved from New York to a house in the husband’s rural Montana hometown.

The air is thick and humid, the decrepit house is big and lonely, and Grace (Lawrence), who gives birth early on in the movie, starts to unravel: there’s both too much to do and too little, and she begins to sink into the quagmire of isolation and postpartum depression as responsibilities of motherhood weigh her down.

Ramsay brings the novel to life with a typically precise, poetic visual and sound design, crafting something of a modern-day Gothic melodrama. Lawrence anchors the film with a performance of controlled hysteria, while Pattinson, Sissy Spacek (who plays Grace’s mother-in-law), and LaKeith Stanfield (as a neighbor who becomes an object of Grace’s fixation) add nuance and texture in supporting roles.

Die My Love is currently playing in theaters. After its premiere at this year’s Cannes Film Festival, I sat down with Ramsay for a chat about its making. She had just lost her mother days before the festival, and grief tinged her thrill at seeing audiences discover the movie.

My condolences about your mother. I’m sure this must be hard to do in the midst of all that.

Yeah, ’cause I was going to invite her here. But it’s okay. I’m at peace with it now. She lived a long life. She was 80. But she had a good mind, and she was funny. It’s always hard. Your mom, you know?

Of course. And your films are about children and mothers. This must be a bit of a head trip.

Yeah [ laughs ]. But in a way, it’s kind of good, because I’m not taking this too seriously. I think the first time I came here I was quite young.

With your graduate short film, Small Deaths (1996), right?

Yeah. I was really nervous. Now I feel a bit more relaxed.

This is your eighth time at Cannes. Not many people have been here eight times.

I feel a bit more like I know the drill. I remember when I came here with We Need to Talk About Kevin (2011), I was super nervous. My husband is a musician, and I held his hand so tight I nearly broke his fingers. He was like, “That’s my guitar hand!” [ laughs ] But this time, I feel quite relaxed. I like the film.

I read the novel by Ariana Harwicz, which the film is based on, on the flight here.

It’s a hard novel to read—to get through—because it jumps through time, and it’s quite dark as well. I didn’t really want to go that way. I changed that, skewered it. I didn’t want to do another Kevin kind of thing. That put me off, to be honest.

I don’t know if I’ve ever recovered from watching We Need to Talk About Kevin .

I know. Funnily enough, I hadn’t had any children then, but now I do. Every time a mother comes up and says, “We watched Kevin ,” I’m like, “I’m sorry!” The way I looked at Die My Love is I wanted to put some humor in there, and I wanted to take some of the ideas, the themes of the novel—the animalistic kind of feeling, the sexual nature of Grace—but make it a love story. A bonkers, crazy love story, rather than a postpartum story. When people say “postpartum,” I’m like, “That’s not a postpartum movie.” It is and it isn’t.

I’d love to hear about how you translated the inner monologue of the novel into a film that keeps us at arm’s length. You’ve worked before with many novels that are told in the first person, and done very interesting things with them. With Die My Love , another filmmaker might have taken the easy route and done voiceover. But you start with this long, remote, static shot of the house; you never give us full access to the heroine’s mind.

I suppose it’s ’cause I started as a painter, and then a photographer. I’d like to be a painter again, actually; that’s my ambition. I think more in pictures than words. And that’s really handy as a filmmaker. I think of a key image. Here, the first thing was, they’re moving into this new house, and maybe they’ve lived in New York before. This is my backstory: he’s been a musician. She’s written a couple of things that got published. The house is free, but it’s in the bloody middle of nowhere.

The conventional thing to do is to shoot the house from outside. And I thought, no, I’ll shoot the house looking at them . And I’ll have them coming into the house, and we’ll do a locked-off shot. So that’s a sort of key image. It’s almost like the house is alive itself. Then you hear the rats, and there’s something a little bit ominous. But there’s hope in it, as well. The husband is saying—we’re going to do this. There’s an office upstairs for you. I’ll get my drum kit. We can do what we like here. So there’s actually hope here, before it falls apart a bit.

You were saying that you wanted to make it a love story. I was very taken by the fact that you don’t justify Grace’s psychosis and sadness, or create villains. Her husband’s trying his best. Many stories like this make the mother-in-law a shrew, but here, she’s empathetic, too. Like you say, there’s hope in the house.

Well, I thought it was much more interesting—rather than make those archetypes, like the mother-in-law and the husband that’s beating her up or something—to show that there’s real love there for her. But there’s just this misunderstanding. She’s a bit of a wild animal. She’s unconventional, almost an anarchist, you know? Kind of smashing the world up, because she’s frustrated. But I didn’t want to justify it with these easy answers. I think she’s bored; she’s got writer’s block; she and her husband are in different universes for a while. She’s just had a baby, and something starts to unravel a little bit.

What I like about all your films is that you really make us confront a kind of unknowability. Even in Kevin , and Morvern Callar (2002), you don’t explain people. There’s an unknowable kernel in people, and you make us really look at that.

That’s something I’m fascinated by. Morvern Callar was the mysterious kind. You never really knew what she’s thinking. The book is all voice, it’s all explaining her thoughts. But I didn’t do a voiceover. She was an inscrutable character, even in the novel. So I felt she should remain inscrutable, like those cowboys in westerns, riding off into the sunset. I co-wrote that movie with one of my best friends [Liana Dognini], who unfortunately died quite young. But we always thought Morvern was like a cowboy. And here I see an anarchist. I see someone who is going to burn the world down. And I think she sees a reflection of herself in her boy, and that’s terrifying.

The novel takes place in France. It’s written by Ariana Harwicz, who’s Argentine…

I met her here, and she’s amazing. She really likes it. I never met her before getting here. I was a bit like, “Oh my god, feels like I burned your book.” But actually, I think she saw that I caught the essence even if it was different.

That’s great! Was the decision to set it in the U.S. yours, or was it made before you came onto the project? Because the book is so rooted in a sense of place, in a particular kind of rural French setting and life, whereas the film feels so American. It feels steeped in the landscapes, the accents, the weather of rural Montana.

It was my decision. I thought that America’s like different countries. You go to New York and then go to Montana, and it’s a whole different ball game. If you’re living in New York and you just moved to the sticks, let’s say, it’s a massive shift. To be displaced in America… you know, a lot of people move because they don’t have enough money, they can’t stay in New York, and stuff like that. The characters get this free house, so they take it. But then she’s like, “What the fuck? I’m in the middle of nowhere. I don’t really have anything.” And probably Pam, the mother-in-law, is the one that does see her the most.

I read in an interview you did with the Criterion Collection that your mother used to watch the melodramas of Douglas Sirk and Hitchcock. There is something about Jennifer Lawrence’s character that reminded me of a classic melodrama heroine.

I love those kinds of movies. Douglas Sirk was actually quite bold, because he was doing women’s stories, where they’re the main character. He was doing loads of taboo stuff, too, you know? I take a lot of inspiration from those kinds of films, to be honest.

There’s just something about her blonde hair and her bangs, and the little pout that she has, that reminded me of those heroines.

You know, we spent a long time with the bangs. At first Jennifer was like, “I don’t want to do bangs.” And I said, “I want you to do bangs. You look shyer.” I felt like, “Oh, she’s going to freak out.” But she didn’t. She was like, “I love it. I love it.” She’s kept it.

That’s just how you saw her?

Yeah, Veronica Lake. You know?

In that same interview with Criterion, the interviewer brought up something else that I found striking: so many of your films have a shot of the character wrapping a lace curtain around their head. And it happens again here. What’s that about? Is that the key to Lynne Ramsay’s mind?

Well, it just happened, when I was doing the recce, that I went upstairs and there was just a beautiful curtain like that. And I don’t know what it is. It’s just maybe an homage to Ratcatcher (1999). But it was the first image I ever wrote. It’s a little theme. I think it’s like a shroud, slightly, you know? And it’s a bit light as well. I mean, in Ratcatcher there’s a playfulness, and then it becomes something darker. And for Grace, she’s inside this place, kind of stuck. So like being in a bell jar or something.

I’m curious about LaKeith Stanfield’s character.

He’s amazing. I’d like to do a film where he’s the main character, actually. But this is quite a small part, and it was great for him to do this. I think he really liked the script and wanted to be part of it. And the character, in the book as well—is he real or not? That’s something I wanted to play with. When Grace sees them in the car park, it’s like, “Oh god, he is real, and he’s got family, and he’s got kids.” Reality bites. People have lives on the outside. And LaKeith’s got such a powerful presence that even if it’s a small part, he really leaves an imprint.

I thought that it’s interesting that there is this Black man and Black family on the edge of this middle-class white woman’s closed-off world. Race is always a part of those classic melodramas, even if it’s not mentioned explicitly.

I think it could have been either Black or white, but I liked that. Because they’ve got a much nicer house. Like, it’s Grace and Jackson [Pattinson’s character] that have got the crappy house. LaKeith’s character probably does architecture or something, like he’s an intellectual. That’s the way I saw it. And when you see the shot of the house LaKeith stays in, it’s a really nice house. It’s just hinted at subtly.

The songs form a whole other kind of script in the film.

Well, I thought, in my backstory, that he was a failed musician, so he’ll have a big record collection. I think you see it at one point. And then I thought, when she’s bored, she just plays the same records again and again, like [Toni Basil’s recording of] “Mickey.” Also, I was working with George [Vjestica] from the Bad Seeds, the guitarist, before I made the film. I had written a lot of songs, because I was getting bored of waiting for films to happen. I thought, I’ll write songs—at least they’re instant, like Polaroids. George comes over to my apartment, I start singing this song, he starts playing. Click! It just worked. We wrote three songs in maybe half an hour. Then he asked me to come into the recording studio. I started singing this song called “Zero,” totally improvised. And that’s what ended up as the punk track at the beginning of the film.

And then I was playing “Love Will Tear Us Apart,” and Raife Burchell, the film’s music supervisor, told me to try singing it. We were in the countryside, and I just recorded it on an iPhone, and he mixed it. I hate my voice, so I tried to change it, but everyone was like, “This is awesome”—and they persuaded me to use it [as the end-credits song].
excerpt_original: In spite of ourselves: the Scottish auteur discusses her latest, a typically precise portrait of an inscrutable character

"刘子川的画作常描绘超现实、经由数字媒介处理的心灵景观中的人类形象，其形态半隐半现于闪烁的氛围中。以《青春》（2025）为例，这是他“新男孩”系列（2020– ）的最新作品，NANZUKA 廊在今年9月举办的第四届东京当代艺博会（Tokyo Gendai 2026）上对其进行了展示。这幅布面油画展现了一位孤独的主角置身于无尽且色彩明快的广阔空间中，其饱和的蓝绿配色让人联想起早期的桌面设计。宽阔、近乎狂热的笔触以流动的轮廓勾勒出主体；他的面孔转向观者，除了一道隐约的嘴唇裂缝外别无五官，而他身躯的一侧则融化为涂抹与色痕。在右上角，一只无形的手从洪流中伸出，仿佛在抓取以太中的某物。《青春》不仅传神地表达了科技驱动时代的异化感，也表现了其沉浸式的吸引力：正如这位虚幻般的个体在动荡的未知中消解形体一样，我们也已经陷入计算机化的领域，任由我们的心智和身体向模拟妥协。画面中还带有一种运动感、速度感，或许还有一种不可避免性，指向了当代生活中加速的自动化和人工智能无情的蚕食。“有时感觉书页被翻得越来越快，”刘子川对我说，“在我们理解完某一页之前，我们已经迈入了下一个章节。”", article_text:
People

New Currents: Zigsen Liu’s Cybernetic Ecologies

ZIGSEN LIU ,

The Rising Stars , 2026, oil on canvas, 170 x 200 x 5 cm (unframed). Copyright the artist. Courtesy NANZUKA, Tokyo.

In his 1982 short story Burning Chrome , William Gibson coined the term “cyberspace,” referring to the “consensual hallucination experienced daily by legitimate operators, in every nation. . . . A graphic representation of data abstracted from the banks of every computer in the human system.” Although Gibson knew little about computers at the time, he described the condition of virtualization as we know it today: the sense of another realm, an electronic vastness that is at once unnerving and utterly engrossing.

Zigsen Liu reifies this perceptual complexity in his luminous paintings. Born in 1992 in Anhui, he is part of China’s “Post-90s generation,” which grew up at the dawn of the Internet age. The nascent days of the World Wide Web—with its spectacular promises and radical, if still rudimentary, capabilities—sparked his interest in how technology might evolve and alter our understanding of time, space, and memory.

ZIGSEN LIU , Youth , 2025, oil on canvas, 120 x 100 x 4 cm, unframed (left); and Children of the Sea , 2026, oil on canvas, 200 x 170 x 5 cm, unframed (right). Copyright the artist. Courtesy NANZUKA, Tokyo.

Liu’s tableaux often depict human figures within surreal, digitally mediated mindscapes, their forms half absorbed by glimmering atmospheres. Take Youth (2025), the latest addition to his New Boy series (2020– ), which NANZUKA showed at the fourth edition of Tokyo Gendai 2026 this September. The oil-on-canvas features a lone protagonist amid an endless, brightly-hued expanse, its saturated blue-and-green palette recalling early desktop designs. Wide, almost frenetic brushstrokes render the subject in fluid contours; his face is turned toward the viewer, featureless apart from the faint slit of a mouth, while one side of his frame dissolves into smears and streaks. In the upper right, a disembodied hand emerges from the torrent, as if reaching for something in the ether. Youth conveys not only the alienation of the tech-driven age but also its immersive pull: just as the phantom-like individual dematerializes into a turbulent unknown, so too have we become enmeshed in a computerized terrain, our minds and bodies yielding to simulation. There is also an impression of motion, velocity, and perhaps inevitability, pointing to accelerated automation and the relentless encroachment of AI on contemporary life. “Sometimes it feels like the pages of a book are being turned faster and faster,” Liu tells me. “Before we have understood one page, we’re already entering the next chapter.”

Large-scale projects like Children of the Sea and The Rising Stars (both 2026) take a more speculative tone, harnessing the numinous quality of a digital zeitgeist. Here, earthly beings, rendered more concretely, inhabit fantastical environments that conjure the immensity of Gibson’s “cyberspace.” In Children of the Sea , a couple perches on a whale above the ocean, holding hands, as a gaunt, hollow-eyed figure looms behind the man and a giant pink-tentacled octopus sidles up against the woman. The Rising Stars is similarly psychedelic, with human characters dwelling on a strange planet in a distant galaxy, surrounded by massive fungal growth. The dreamlike scenery evokes what British anthropologist Alfred Gell called the “enchantment of technology”: the more esoteric an innovation, the greater our awe. Liu applies this phenomenon to paintings that compel and entrap the gaze as they imagine a future in which spatiotemporal logic and organic matter collapse into a new, cybernetic ecology.

Annette Meier is an assistant editor at ArtAsiaPacific.

"在她家的客厅里，光线透过美好年代风格的彩色玻璃窗洒进来。在我们交谈的丝绒沙发后面，立着一个由她孩子制作的纸板迪士尼角色（《阿拉丁》中的大反派贾法尔），周围则以一种井然有序的杂货铺风格摆放着各种画作、素描、绘画或照片。露易丝·布尔戈因的居所兼具公寓与工作室的双重特质，既禅意又温馨，它证明了一件事：在这里，古典艺术、人体素描和儿童涂鸦之间没有任何阶级之分。在埃米莉·诺布莱执导的《Bis "面对摄像机，她朗读着有趣、大胆、精明且另类的台词，同时化身为一个性感的节目主持人，并带有这种角色可能带来的局限性和刻板化。露易丝·布尔戈因一点也没有否认这段电视经历——同样，这里没有阶级之分，也没有多少评判。必须承认，她在电视上的表演有一个长处，那就是证明了这个好学生——她会在开拍前很久就用方法背诵台词（她会抄写台词，然后通过颠倒句子中的词语来记住台词）——在银幕上展现某种离经叛道时，反而表现得极其出色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "活雕像“这是一位对我影响很大的艺术家，”当被问及她与著名且具有挑衅性的法国艺术家路易斯·布尔吉奥的关系时，露易丝·布尔戈因告诉我们，她正是从这位艺术家身上汲取灵感，才有了自己的女演员艺名。“我在17岁时发现了她，后来我看了一部纪录片，片中她在削一个橙子，并以一种惊人的方式谈论她的作品。她装作天真地说，她那些巨大的雪花石膏阴茎其实是戴着高领毛衣的小女孩。她嘲笑观众，并在谈论自己的作品时表现出一种无礼。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在《Bis repetita》的一个场景中，学生们和他们的老师参观了那不勒斯遗址，面对古代裸体雕塑，脸上流露出半是被惊到、半是被逗乐的神情。在片场之外，裸体恰恰是露易丝·布尔戈因热衷的主题。2012年，她与埃德瓦尔·米诺（Edwart Minot）合著了《奥赛博物馆大解密》（Orsay mis à nu），在这本书中她对奥赛博物馆中最美的赤裸艺术品进行了评点。“我一直很喜欢画交织、拥抱的身体。我不喜欢画衣服，因为那会让作品带有年代感。在这本书中，我聚焦于19世纪末和20世纪初的作品，里面女性画家很少，但女性裸体模特远多于男性模特。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "绘画与电影，异曲同工？这位女演员在银幕很长一段时间里都被局限于缪斯的角色（诱惑者或恋爱中的角色），她喜欢扮演“那些不太光彩、会作弊、会撒谎的人”，年轻时曾深受拉里·克拉克（Larry Clark）或格雷格·阿拉基（Gregg Araki）电影的震撼，如今她似乎终于迎来了与其气场（参见托马斯·利尔蒂的电视剧《希波克拉底》，她在其中饰演了一名才华横溢、雄心勃勃的实习医生）以及喜剧爆发力（参见《Bis repetita》中她那些堪称典故的醉酒场景）相称的角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这位四十多岁的女演员远非处于危机之中，恰恰相反，她迎来了一种艺术上的圆满——2022年，她首次勇敢地在劳拉·佩舍尔画廊（galerie Laura Derrière le canapé en velours sur lequel on discute, il y a un personnage de Disney (le vilain Jafar, dans Aladdin) en carton, fabriqué par son enfant, et, tout autour, des dessins, croquis, peintures ou photos, disposés dans une sorte de bazar ordonné. À mi-chemin entre un appartement et un atelier, l’intérieur de l’habitation de Louise Bourgoin, zen et chaleureuse, atteste d’une chose : ici, pas de hiérarchie entre l’art classique, les dessins de nus et les gribouillages enfantins. Dans Bis repetita d’Émilie Noblet, il y a une combinaison tout aussi grisante entre totems antiques et culture pop (on apprend les rudiments du latin en écoutant sur YouTube une version traduite en latin de « Pour que tu m’aimes encore » , le hit sentimental de Céline Dion)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "L’actrice y campe avec une jubilation contagieuse Delphine, une prof démissionnaire d’un lycée d’Angers. C’était une grande responsabilité de l’incarner à l’écran. »"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Pas vraiment du genre dissipée à l’école ( « j’avais quand même la pression pour ne pas redoubler, ça aurait été horrible pour mes parents » ) ni dégoûtée par ce métier, la future actrice, attirée par les arts plastiques, cherche d’abord à marcher dans les pas de sa famille. article_text:
Ce portrait a été initialement publié en 2024, lors de la sortie du folm,

Dans son salon, la lumière passe à travers des fenêtres en vitrail typiques de la Belle Époque. Derrière le canapé en velours sur lequel on discute, il y a un personnage de Disney (le vilain Jafar, dans Aladdin) en carton, fabriqué par son enfant, et, tout autour, des dessins, croquis, peintures ou photos, disposés dans une sorte de bazar ordonné. À mi-chemin entre un appartement et un atelier, l’intérieur de l’habitation de Louise Bourgoin, zen et chaleureuse, atteste d’une chose : ici, pas de hiérarchie entre l’art classique, les dessins de nus et les gribouillages enfantins. Dans Bis repetita d’Émilie Noblet, il y a une combinaison tout aussi grisante entre totems antiques et culture pop (on apprend les rudiments du latin en écoutant sur YouTube une version traduite en latin de « Pour que tu m’aimes encore » , le hit sentimental de Céline Dion).

L’actrice y campe avec une jubilation contagieuse Delphine, une prof démissionnaire d’un lycée d’Angers. Pas très à cheval sur la déontologie, celle-ci scrolle les offres de fringues sur des applications face à des élèves désintéressés au possible. Les deux parties ont passé un contrat : contre des 19 sur 20 dans les bulletins de notes pipés, les élèves laissent leur prof tranquille. Tout ce beau monde blasé doit remettre le pied à l’étrier quand la directrice (la géniale Noémie Lvovsky), les croyant surdoués, inscrit les élèves au championnat international de latin, à Naples.

Hasard du calendrier : en moins d’un an, Louise Bourgoin a campé deux profs au bout du rouleau, d’abord dans un registre plus grave chez Thomas Lilti, dans Un métier sérieux , et maintenant chez Émilie Noblet. Si elle interprète si bien ces enseignantes au bord de la crise de nerfs, c’est aussi parce qu’elle connaît par cœur et intimement ce milieu.

« Un métier sérieux » de Thomas Lilti : l’école au corps

AU PREMIER RANG

L’actrice, qui arbore une marinière (comme un subtil clin d’œil à ses origines bretonnes, elle qui est née à Rennes en 1981), avait tout pour être une enfant de la balle : sa mère était prof de lettres modernes ; son père, de philosophie. En grandissant, elle les a vus trimer : « Ils étaient régulièrement épuisés par leur travail. Et j’ai grandi dans les années 1990-2000, donc ce n’est pas un phénomène nouveau, même si on en parle plus aujourd’hui. C’est un métier extrêmement peu considéré en France, difficile, sous-payé. C’était une grande responsabilité de l’incarner à l’écran. »

Pas vraiment du genre dissipée à l’école ( « j’avais quand même la pression pour ne pas redoubler, ça aurait été horrible pour mes parents » ) ni dégoûtée par ce métier, la future actrice, attirée par les arts plastiques, cherche d’abord à marcher dans les pas de sa famille. Elle suit des études aux Beaux-Arts. Elle tente de rentrer dans le moule familial en s’inscrivant comme prof stagiaire à l’Institut universitaire de formation des maîtres, en vue de passer son CAPES. C’est après avoir échoué au concours qu’elle décide de passer des castings pour la télé et le cinéma.

Rétrospectivement, ce lancement dans le jeu sans filet ni formation a provoqué un complexe durable chez elle. « C’est un métier un peu magique parce que quelqu’un comme moi, qui n’a pas pris de cours, peut démarrer avec un premier rôle. Mais j’ai un sentiment d’illégitimité, je culpabilise de ne pas avoir fait le Conservatoire. » La première fois que le public la découvre, c’est sur le plateau du Grand Journal de Canal+, en 2006, où elle officie comme Miss météo.

Xavier Lacaille : « Quand je n’arrive pas à mettre mon masque social, ça me tord profondément »

Face caméra, elle lit des textes drôles, osés, malins et décalés, tout en entrant dans la peau d’une animatrice sexy, avec les limites et la stéréotypisation que ce rôle peut engendrer. Louise Bourgoin ne renie pas du tout cette expérience à la télévision – là encore, pas de hiérarchie, et peu de jugement. Il faut dire que ses performances télévisuelles ont eu le mérite de montrer que cette bonne élève, qui apprend ses textes longtemps avant le tournage et avec méthode (elle les recopie, puis mémorise les répliques en inversant les mots dans les phrases), excelle paradoxalement à incarner une forme d’irrévérence à l’écran.

STATUES VIVANTES « C’est une artiste qui m’a beaucoup marquée » , nous dit Louise Bourgoin quand on l’interroge sur son rapport à Louise Bourgeois, artiste française célèbre et provocante, dont elle s’est inspirée pour trouver son pseudonyme d’actrice. « Je l’ai découverte à mes 17 ans, puis j’ai regardé un documentaire dans lequel elle épluche une orange et parle de façon étonnante de son travail. Elle joue la naïve en disant que ses immenses phallus en albâtre sont des petites filles avec des cols roulés. Elle se moque des spectateurs et a une insolence dans son discours sur ses œuvres. »

Dans une scène de Bis repetita , les élèves et leur prof visitent les ruines napolitaines et bloquent sur des sculptures antiques de nus, avec un air mi-choqué, mi-amusé. Hors plateau, le nu passionne justement Louise Bourgoin. En 2012, elle a coécrit avec Edwart Minot Orsay mis à nu , livre dans lequel elle commente les plus belles œuvres déshabillées du musée d’Orsay. « J’ai toujours adoré dessiner des corps entremêlés, enlacés. Je n’aime pas dessiner des vêtements, parce que ça date une œuvre. Dans le livre, je me suis penchée sur des œuvres de la fin du xixe et du début du xxe siècle, avec peu de peintres femmes mais beaucoup plus de modèles féminins nus que masculins. »

Peinture et cinéma, même combat ? Longtemps cantonnée sur le grand écran à des rôles de muses (des personnages de séductrices ou d’amoureuses), l’actrice, qui aime jouer « des personnes pas très reluisantes, qui trichent, qui mentent » et qui a été chamboulée plus jeune par les films de Larry Clark ou Gregg Araki, semble enfin avoir droit à des rôles à la hauteur de son aura (voir la série Hippocrate de Thomas Lilti, dans laquelle elle incarne une interne en médecine brillante et ambitieuse) et de sa puissance comique (voir ses scènes alcoolisées dans Bis repetita , anthologiques).

Loin d’être en crise, la quadra atteint a contrario une forme de plénitude artistique – elle a osé exposer pour la première fois ses œuvres à la galerie Laura Pecheur, en 2022. Elle espère secrètement se lancer dans l’arène de films d’action (elle fait de la boxe française) : « J’aime beaucoup la violence féminine au cinéma, elle est encore trop rare. » À voir son visage anguleux et son regard féroce lorsqu’elle ne sourit pas, on se dit qu’elle pourrait tout pulvériser.

Bis repetita d’Émilie Noblet, Le Pacte (1h26), sortie le 20 mars.

"该展览深入概括了这位艺术家的作品，主要聚焦于拉丁美洲的文化历史。伊图尔比德的视觉世界探索了生命与死亡、仪式以及日常生活体验等普遍主题，其特点是具有动人的诗意和魔力。这位摄影师突出了文化与自然、传统与现代、身份与表征之间的张力，确保她的影像保持着一种神秘的模糊性。格拉谢拉·伊图尔比德深深扎根于墨西哥原住民文化，并将超现实主义元素与宗教和神秘主义融合在一起，在几十年里发展出了一种无可模仿的视觉语言——主要以黑白为主。鸟类和面具作为象征性的伴侣一次又一次地出现。这位摄影师最著名的作品是令人惊叹的“Nuestra Vogel）于2019年获此殊荣，拉尔夫·吉布森（Ralph Gibson）于2021年获奖，艾略特·厄威特（Elliott Erwitt）于2023年获奖，海琳德·柯尔布（Herlinde Koelbl）于2024年获奖。随着格拉谢拉·伊图尔比德的加入，入选徕卡名人堂的成员总数已达到15人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "She is the most famous contemporary Mexican photographer in the world: this year, Graciela Iturbide has been awarded the “Leica Hall of Fame” prize for her entire body of work. The award ceremony took place as part of the “Celebration of Photography” on October 8, 2026 at Leica World in Wetzlar. The accompanying exhibition, presenting more than 50 photographs, will be on view at the Leica Gallery in Wetzlar until January 2027. Iturbide’s photograph “Na’ Lupe Pan,” from the series “Juchitán,” Oaxaca, Mexico, 1986, has been chosen as the “Leica Picture of the Year 2026.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The exhibition offers an in-depth overview of the artist’s work, devoted mainly to Latin American cultural history. Exploring universal themes such as life and death, rituals and the experiences of everyday life, Iturbide’s visual universe is characterized by its moving poetry and magic. The photographer highlights the tensions between culture and nature, tradition and modernity, identity and representation, ensuring that her images retain an enigmatic ambiguity. Deeply rooted in Mexican indigenous culture and blending surrealist elements with religion and mysticism, Graciela Iturbide has developed, over many decades, an inimitable visual language – mainly in black and white. Birds and masks appear again and again as symbolic companions. article_text:
She is the most famous contemporary Mexican photographer in the world: this year, Graciela Iturbide has been awarded the “Leica Hall of Fame” prize for her entire body of work. The award ceremony took place as part of the “Celebration of Photography” on October 8, 2026 at Leica World in Wetzlar. The accompanying exhibition, presenting more than 50 photographs, will be on view at the Leica Gallery in Wetzlar until January 2027. Iturbide’s photograph “Na’ Lupe Pan,” from the series “Juchitán,” Oaxaca, Mexico, 1986, has been chosen as the “Leica Picture of the Year 2026.”

The exhibition offers an in-depth overview of the artist’s work, devoted mainly to Latin American cultural history. Exploring universal themes such as life and death, rituals and the experiences of everyday life, Iturbide’s visual universe is characterized by its moving poetry and magic. The photographer highlights the tensions between culture and nature, tradition and modernity, identity and representation, ensuring that her images retain an enigmatic ambiguity. Deeply rooted in Mexican indigenous culture and blending surrealist elements with religion and mysticism, Graciela Iturbide has developed, over many decades, an inimitable visual language – mainly in black and white. Birds and masks appear again and again as symbolic companions. The photographer’s best-known work, the astonishing “Nuestra Señora de las iguanas” (Our Lady of the Iguanas), was taken in 1979 in a market in Juchitán. It is a mysterious portrait of a female vendor wearing a crown of live iguanas: a Mexican hydra, but also, in the Christian interpretation, a female figure of Christ wearing a crown of thorns of an animal nature.

Graciela Iturbide’s photographic work belongs to a humanist tradition that incorporates psychological and spiritual elements, transforming the documentary image into a form of subjective photography of extraordinary richness and nuance. Besides her still lifes and landscapes, it is her social reportage on the living conditions of Mexico’s indigenous communities and on the importance of matriarchal social structures that caused a stir and established her as one of the most important photographic voices in Latin America.

The exhibition organized on the sidelines of the Leica Hall of Fame Award presentation brings together more than 50 photographs from five series: “Juchitán,” with pictures of this Mexican town in the state of Oaxaca (1979–1988), “México Clásicas” (1974–2008), “Pájaros” (Birds, 1987–1998), “Desierto de Sonora” (1979) and “Viajes” (Journeys), made in Ecuador, Panama, Argentina and Cuba (1972–1994).

Graciela Iturbide was born in Mexico City on May 16, 1942. Even as a child she was fascinated by photography: her father was a passionate amateur photographer. She married the architect Manuel Rocha Díaz (1936–1996) at the age of 19 and became the mother of three children. In 1969, she began studying film at the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM), at the Centro Universitario de Estudios Cinematográficos (CUEC). In 1970, she spent a year as an assistant to photographer Manuel Álvarez Bravo, whom she accompanied on many trips, discovering rural Mexico and the diversity of its indigenous communities. A stroke of fate, the death of her six-year-old daughter Claudia, radically upended Graciela Iturbide’s life, and she then chose to become a professional photographer. In 1975, she had her first exhibition in Mexico City, followed by her first in New York in 1976. From the 1980s onward, she began to gain international recognition. She has received numerous awards, including the W. Eugene Smith Grant (1987), the Hugo Erfurth Prize (1989), the Prix des Rencontres internationales de la photographie d’Arles (1991), the Hasselblad Award (2008), the gold medal of the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura (INBAL) in Mexico City (2024) and the Princess of Asturias Award for the Arts (2025). Iturbide lives in Mexico City.

Leica Picture of the Year sold exclusively in Leica Galleries

An exclusive limited-edition photograph by Graciela Iturbide is available in Leica Galleries around the world as the “Leica Picture of the Year 2026.” The image, titled “Na’ Lupe Pan” and taken in Oaxaca, Mexico, in 1986, is part of the series “Juchitán.” Since 2021, Leica Camera AG has awarded the “Leica Picture of the Year” to exceptional Leica photographers who have been inducted into the Leica Hall of Fame. Following in the footsteps of Ralph Gibson, Thomas Hoepker, Elliott Erwitt, Herlinde Koelbl and Joel Meyerowitz, Graciela Iturbide is the photographer behind the 2026 “Leica Picture of the Year.”

The Leica Gallery in Paris (26 rue Boissy d’Anglas – 75008) will sell 3 prints starting in December 2026.

Special print price: €1,500 incl. VAT

Leica Hall of Fame Award

Images that have moved the world, moments that will remain forever engraved in memory: since 2011, Leica Camera AG has been inducting exceptional photographers into the Leica Hall of Fame – photographers whose view of the world made a difference and served as a vehicle for change. These emblematic images, now anchored in collective memory, bear witness to their work, touch the viewer and illustrate the “human condition” in a timeless way. Steve McCurry was the first to receive the Leica Hall of Fame Award in 2011, followed by Barbara Klemm, Nick Út, René Burri, Thomas Hoepker and Ara Güler. Joel Meyerowitz was honored in 2016, Gianni Berengo Gardin in 2017, then Bruce Davidson and Jürgen Schadeberg in 2018. Walter Vogel followed in 2019, Ralph Gibson in 2021, Elliott Erwitt in 2023 and Herlinde Koelbl in 2024. With the arrival of Graciela Iturbide, the number of members inducted into the Leica Hall of Fame now stands at 15.

At the “Celebration of Photography” held on October 8 at Leica World in Wetzlar, Graciela Iturbide’s induction into the Leica Hall of Fame was not the only highlight: the winners of the 46th Leica Oskar Barnack Award, as well as those of the LOBA Women Grant – awarded for the first time – were also honored. In addition, all the shortlisted series for LOBA 2026 are on display at the Ernst Leitz Museum until February 18, 2027.

article_text:
Action drama-thriller “Unguarded,” the second movie as a director of Mario Casas , toplined by Mario and Óscar Casas as underground bare-knuckle MMA fighters, will be brought to market by Film Factory Ent. at this week’s AFM.

Film Factory will handle international sales.

International star Mario Casas (“The Invisible Guest,” “Cross the Line,” “Bird Box Barcelona)” leads a powerful talent and producer-distribution package of writer Eduard Sola (“A House on Fire,” “Querer”), star Oscar Casas (“Idols”) and producer Nostromo Pictures (“Monitor,” “Apocalipsis Z,” “The Invisible Guest”) and A puño descubierto AIE. Nostromo produces in association with Movistar Plus+ (“La Bola Negra,” “The Beloved” and “Sirāt”) with the participation of HBO Max.

Related Stories

Animated Movie ‘Apple Cadabra – I Shrunk Myself’ Boarded by Epsilon Film (EXCLUSIVE)

Heaven's Gate Cult Thriller 'The Leader,' Starring Vera Farmiga, Tim Blake Nelson and Jim Parsons, Bought for U.S. by Dark Sky Films (EXCLUSIVE)

Warner Bros. Pictures will release the film theatrically in Spain in 2027.

Described as a grounded, high-intensity action drama and a raw and emotional story of brotherhood, guilt and survival, “Unguarded” (“A puño descubierto”) turns on Luis, who survives in the world of underground fighting world alongside brother Daniel, whose fraternal bond is called “as strong as it is fragile.”

One sibling dreams of escape, the other remains trapped. “Caught between loyalty, necessity and difficult decisions, both must face their own limits. ‘Unguarded’ is a story about brotherhood, sacrifice and the possibility (or impossibility) of escaping an inherited destiny,” the synopsis runs.

Tania Noriega (“Lady Altagracia”), Migdalia H. and Javier Oliveras complete the cast.

Shot with two cameras and long takes hugging the actors and lasting in some cases as much as 20 or 30 minutes – which allows Mario Casas to remain onscreen and adds a larger realism to scenes, he has commented – “Unguarded” went into production in April shooting for six-and-a half-weeks in lesser known parts of Barcelona, with some fight scenes lensing on Canary Island Gran Canaria.

Fight sequences were choreographed to capture the reality of such combat. Óscar Casas trained intensively for months alongside combat-sports professionals to prepare for the role.

That said, “This is not a fight movie,” said Casas. “It’s about how two brothers relate to violence. We are following the characters all the time, creating a real place. What I want is for the shoot to feel alive. I’m very happy to be telling this second story as a director.”

“We are delighted to team up again with Nostromo and to accompany Mario Casas on his second film as a director,” said Film Factory Director Vicente Canales.

“‘Unguarded’ is an intense, emotional and deeply physical story, powered by the unique chemistry between Mario and Óscar Casas, and we are convinced it will connect strongly with audiences and buyers worldwide,” Canales added.

title_original: Spy catchers: Valeria Arendar and Eleana Konstantellos uncover Mexican espionage in the Cold War era
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "From the series The Dice Was Loaded from the Start © Valeria Arendar and Eleana Konstantellos."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "In The Dice Was Loaded from the Start , Valeria Arendar and Eleana Konstantellos trace and reconstruct a history of espionage in Mexico."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "From the glamorous exploits of James Bond to the quiet calculations of George Smiley, popular culture has fashioned the spy into a fascinating character. Cinema and fiction in particular have created an imaginary of espionage defined by secrecy, power and shifting identities. But little is known about how intelligence work is actually conducted, particularly outside the West. The Dice Was Loaded from the Start is an ongoing project by Mexican photographers Valeria Arendar and Eleana Konstantellos which traces the infrastructures of espionage in Mexico at the height of the Cold War."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Collating archival images, forensic still lifes, unfamiliar apparatuses and staged photographs, The Dice Was Loaded from the Start weaves together the fragmented narrative of Mexico’s role in the Cold War. The geopolitical tension between the United States and the Soviet Union sucked in the rest of the world, from the aftermath of World War Two until the dissolution of the USSR in 1991. Both superpowers sought to expand their spheres of influence and advance competing capitalist and communist ideologies through proxy wars, expanding nuclear arsenals, and the Space Race pursuit of technological supremacy."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ArendarKonstantellos_19.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "From the series The Dice Was Loaded from the Start © Valeria Arendar and Eleana Konstantellos.", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ArendarKonstantellos_14.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "From the series The Dice Was Loaded from the Start © Valeria Arendar and Eleana Konstantellos.", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "quote", "text": "“Photography is always a secondary character in espionage, and we realised it would be interesting to incorporate the medium itself, to create a kind of meta-project through analogue photography and all its different components” – Eleana Konstantellos"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These efforts relied on expansive espionage networks, intelligence agencies and covert operations. And by maintaining diplomatic relationships with the United States and the Soviet Union, including hosting both countries’ embassies in its capital, Mexico became a crucial node in the CIA and KGB’s work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Arendar and Konstantellos first encountered the history of espionage in Mexico while researching political events from the 1970s and 1980s. Both artists have individual practices rooted in the history and politics of 20th century Latin America, grounded in their own family histories. Arendar’s heritage is Russian, Argentinian and Mexican, while Konstantellos’ is Greek, French and Mexican; their joint project subtly acknowledges these intertwined stories with an image depicting their families’ passports."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Their shared interests made the history of espionage in Mexico fertile ground for a collaboration. It is also an important untold story. Despite the extensive presence and influence of two of the most powerful intelligence agencies, little is known about what happened in Mexico. Operation LITEMPO was a powerful covert operation run by the CIA in the country, for example, and, according to the artists; “It is even said that all Mexican presidents who were in charge of the country between 1958 and 1988 were recruited by the US Intelligence Agency (CIA).”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Arendar and Konstantellos’ project sits in the blurry boundaries of fact and fiction. It is grounded in extensive records produced by the Dirección Federal de Seguridad (Federal Security Directorate), now held at the Archivo General de la Nación (General Archive of the Nation). Commonly known as the secret police, the Dirección Federal de Seguridad was created with the support of the CIA and operated for more than 35 years."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“There are millions of records, most of them ridiculous and registering people’s daily routines,” says Arendar. “For example, if you travelled to Cuba… you were automatically labelled a communist, a subversive, and needed to be under surveillance. I think the accumulation of all these seemingly innocuous files created an atmosphere of paranoia within Mexico’s so-called democracy.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ArendarKonstantellos_3.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "From the series The Dice Was Loaded from the Start © Valeria Arendar and Eleana Konstantellos.", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ArendarKonstantellos_9.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "from the series The Dice Was Loaded from the Start © Valeria Arendar and Eleana Konstantellos.", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The duo’s findings in the Archivo General de la Nación inform one of their photographic approaches – staged visual interpretations of the contexts surrounding the archival records, which they present in dialogue with historical images. Combining sharp humour and play, the artists reflect on the Mexican government’s extreme obsession with tracing citizens. In one of the photographs, we see a young man smoking in a business suit, for example, while his height is being measured with an L-shaped ruler."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We approached the project as a kind of game, and that’s really what’s behind the practice,” says Konstantellos. “The staging, the fiction, dressing up and stepping into different roles, as a way of trying to understand the gaps in the official histories – and, in a sense, filling them.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Elsewhere Arendar and Konstantellos let the archive speak for itself, inviting viewers to interpret the wider histories it suggests. “A lot of the files might seem overwhelming and make you wonder, what did they use them for?” says Konstantellos. “Often, the information in them turned into torture, disappearances, and a whole host of things that are much more intense – things that we often omit, that we don’t quite know how to handle within the project, because they are very delicate.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "An image of one of the students killed during the 1968 Tlatelolco massacre reflects on the relationship between surveillance, state violence and enforced disappearance. In the lead-up to the Summer Olympics in Mexico City, numerous non-violent demonstrators took to the streets, protesting authoritarian rule, political repression and social inequality. Framed by Mexican President Gustavo Díaz Ordaz as a ‘communist conspiracy’, the demonstrations were met with military force. Soldiers and police opened fire on unarmed civilians."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Arendar and Konstantellos’ second photographic approach focuses on espionage kit. Combining technology associated with analogue photography, and research into the collection of the German Spy Museum, the artists have created a catalogue of surveillance tools that might have been used by the KGB in Mexico."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Photography is a fundamental part of espionage,” says Konstantellos. “It is direct proof that someone entered a house at a particular time, or that an exchange of information took place. Photography is always a secondary character in espionage, and we realised it would be interesting to incorporate the medium itself, to create a kind of meta-project through analogue photography and all its different components.” Set against cold, sterile backdrops in greyscale or dramatic scenes lit through chiaroscuro, these images evoke the political tension, secrecy and anxiety of the time."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ArendarKonstantellos_31.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Agents of the Soviet Union’s Central Intelligence Department used this scope for nighttime training raids across their embassy located in Mexico City. \nIt was taken from a captured KGB spy.", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ArendarKonstantellos_30.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "During the 1970s, US military intelligence used communications jammers, a radio frequency device. When activated, this device would jam all radio communications around it then self detonate after its cycle was complete. It was used to spy on well-known intellectuals such as Carlos Fuentes.", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "More recently Arendar and Konstantellos have shifted their attention from the most familiar features of espionage – namely gadgets and men. There were also covert networks of intelligence-gathering in Mexico, they point out, within which women worked. “After a pause, we returned to the project and decided to focus on the role of women within this ecosystem,” says Arendar. “We didn’t want to be two women photographing more male spies, as Hollywood has done, so we decided to approach the project through a gender perspective. The structures that made espionage possible included secretaries, receptionists, telephone operators, the wives of diplomats and so on – all roles that remained largely invisible. We call them the unconscious army of espionage.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Women carrying briefcases, women handling and passing documents, women climbing staircases, women moving files from one place to another, women listening in, women at hairdressing salons, women at home. All but one look away in the images, emphasising the secondary role women have occupied in histories of espionage – but paradoxically casting them as indispensable. After all, the most effective spies are ones you never know about."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The gradual disappearance of faces accompanies a shift in the project,” the artists explain. “Individual identities cease to be the centre of attention, giving way to a reflection on those anonymous presences that sustain the system from the margins.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And in this another meta-layer emerges – Arendar and Konstantellos both perform for the camera, and so their authorship disappears. The viewer is left to wonder who is photographing whom. “Our physical resemblance plays into this ambiguity, and we want this uncertainty to be part of the experience of the images,” they explain."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Dice Was Loaded from the Start reflects on past events but in doing so it also speaks of persisting methods. article_text:
From the series The Dice Was Loaded from the Start © Valeria Arendar and Eleana Konstantellos.

In The Dice Was Loaded from the Start , Valeria Arendar and Eleana Konstantellos trace and reconstruct a history of espionage in Mexico.

From the glamorous exploits of James Bond to the quiet calculations of George Smiley, popular culture has fashioned the spy into a fascinating character. Cinema and fiction in particular have created an imaginary of espionage defined by secrecy, power and shifting identities. But little is known about how intelligence work is actually conducted, particularly outside the West. The Dice Was Loaded from the Start is an ongoing project by Mexican photographers Valeria Arendar and Eleana Konstantellos which traces the infrastructures of espionage in Mexico at the height of the Cold War.

Collating archival images, forensic still lifes, unfamiliar apparatuses and staged photographs, The Dice Was Loaded from the Start weaves together the fragmented narrative of Mexico’s role in the Cold War. The geopolitical tension between the United States and the Soviet Union sucked in the rest of the world, from the aftermath of World War Two until the dissolution of the USSR in 1991. Both superpowers sought to expand their spheres of influence and advance competing capitalist and communist ideologies through proxy wars, expanding nuclear arsenals, and the Space Race pursuit of technological supremacy.

“Photography is always a secondary character in espionage, and we realised it would be interesting to incorporate the medium itself, to create a kind of meta-project through analogue photography and all its different components” – Eleana Konstantellos

These efforts relied on expansive espionage networks, intelligence agencies and covert operations. And by maintaining diplomatic relationships with the United States and the Soviet Union, including hosting both countries’ embassies in its capital, Mexico became a crucial node in the CIA and KGB’s work.

Arendar and Konstantellos first encountered the history of espionage in Mexico while researching political events from the 1970s and 1980s. Both artists have individual practices rooted in the history and politics of 20th century Latin America, grounded in their own family histories. Arendar’s heritage is Russian, Argentinian and Mexican, while Konstantellos’ is Greek, French and Mexican; their joint project subtly acknowledges these intertwined stories with an image depicting their families’ passports.

Their shared interests made the history of espionage in Mexico fertile ground for a collaboration. It is also an important untold story. Despite the extensive presence and influence of two of the most powerful intelligence agencies, little is known about what happened in Mexico. Operation LITEMPO was a powerful covert operation run by the CIA in the country, for example, and, according to the artists; “It is even said that all Mexican presidents who were in charge of the country between 1958 and 1988 were recruited by the US Intelligence Agency (CIA).”

Arendar and Konstantellos’ project sits in the blurry boundaries of fact and fiction. It is grounded in extensive records produced by the Dirección Federal de Seguridad (Federal Security Directorate), now held at the Archivo General de la Nación (General Archive of the Nation). Commonly known as the secret police, the Dirección Federal de Seguridad was created with the support of the CIA and operated for more than 35 years.

“There are millions of records, most of them ridiculous and registering people’s daily routines,” says Arendar. “For example, if you travelled to Cuba… you were automatically labelled a communist, a subversive, and needed to be under surveillance. I think the accumulation of all these seemingly innocuous files created an atmosphere of paranoia within Mexico’s so-called democracy.”

The duo’s findings in the Archivo General de la Nación inform one of their photographic approaches – staged visual interpretations of the contexts surrounding the archival records, which they present in dialogue with historical images. Combining sharp humour and play, the artists reflect on the Mexican government’s extreme obsession with tracing citizens. In one of the photographs, we see a young man smoking in a business suit, for example, while his height is being measured with an L-shaped ruler.

“We approached the project as a kind of game, and that’s really what’s behind the practice,” says Konstantellos. “The staging, the fiction, dressing up and stepping into different roles, as a way of trying to understand the gaps in the official histories – and, in a sense, filling them.”

Elsewhere Arendar and Konstantellos let the archive speak for itself, inviting viewers to interpret the wider histories it suggests. “A lot of the files might seem overwhelming and make you wonder, what did they use them for?” says Konstantellos. “Often, the information in them turned into torture, disappearances, and a whole host of things that are much more intense – things that we often omit, that we don’t quite know how to handle within the project, because they are very delicate.”

An image of one of the students killed during the 1968 Tlatelolco massacre reflects on the relationship between surveillance, state violence and enforced disappearance. In the lead-up to the Summer Olympics in Mexico City, numerous non-violent demonstrators took to the streets, protesting authoritarian rule, political repression and social inequality. Framed by Mexican President Gustavo Díaz Ordaz as a ‘communist conspiracy’, the demonstrations were met with military force. Soldiers and police opened fire on unarmed civilians.

Arendar and Konstantellos’ second photographic approach focuses on espionage kit. Combining technology associated with analogue photography, and research into the collection of the German Spy Museum, the artists have created a catalogue of surveillance tools that might have been used by the KGB in Mexico.

“Photography is a fundamental part of espionage,” says Konstantellos. “It is direct proof that someone entered a house at a particular time, or that an exchange of information took place. Photography is always a secondary character in espionage, and we realised it would be interesting to incorporate the medium itself, to create a kind of meta-project through analogue photography and all its different components.” Set against cold, sterile backdrops in greyscale or dramatic scenes lit through chiaroscuro, these images evoke the political tension, secrecy and anxiety of the time.

More recently Arendar and Konstantellos have shifted their attention from the most familiar features of espionage – namely gadgets and men. There were also covert networks of intelligence-gathering in Mexico, they point out, within which women worked. “After a pause, we returned to the project and decided to focus on the role of women within this ecosystem,” says Arendar. “We didn’t want to be two women photographing more male spies, as Hollywood has done, so we decided to approach the project through a gender perspective. The structures that made espionage possible included secretaries, receptionists, telephone operators, the wives of diplomats and so on – all roles that remained largely invisible. We call them the unconscious army of espionage.”

Women carrying briefcases, women handling and passing documents, women climbing staircases, women moving files from one place to another, women listening in, women at hairdressing salons, women at home. All but one look away in the images, emphasising the secondary role women have occupied in histories of espionage – but paradoxically casting them as indispensable. After all, the most effective spies are ones you never know about.

“The gradual disappearance of faces accompanies a shift in the project,” the artists explain. “Individual identities cease to be the centre of attention, giving way to a reflection on those anonymous presences that sustain the system from the margins.”

And in this another meta-layer emerges – Arendar and Konstantellos both perform for the camera, and so their authorship disappears. The viewer is left to wonder who is photographing whom. “Our physical resemblance plays into this ambiguity, and we want this uncertainty to be part of the experience of the images,” they explain.

The Dice Was Loaded from the Start reflects on past events but in doing so it also speaks of persisting methods. Konstantellos claims the relevance of these topics nowadays, especially around surveillance. “They still raise the same key questions,” she says. “Espionage is one of the most current issues we’re experiencing, and being able to discuss it from the perspective of the past helps people gain some distance and reflect on it.”

The project also invites us to consider how espionage mutates and morphs, and how we are all implicated in it. In one photograph, two women sit beneath hooded hairdryers, apparently listening intently. This image fictionalises the lives of diplomats’ wives and their possible roles in intelligence, but of course there are parallels with the everyday. “We’ve all gone to the hairdresser and eavesdropped,” smiles Arendar. “You don’t set out to do it, but it has become normal.

“Another example is on the subway. You glance at the person’s phone sitting next to you and see a conversation, then you find out something you shouldn’t have. It is interesting how these small acts very much echo espionage.”

The history of photography has long been accompanied by binaries of fact and fiction. But while photographs are often interpreted in terms of evidence, The Dice Was Loaded from the Start positions them as tools for speculation and reconstruction. Ultimately, it aims to give visual form to histories that the archives cannot fully reveal. Fictionalising these histories does not imply reaching definitive answers, but recognising the unrecorded possibilities of the past. “What’s interesting about fiction is that it also helps us think about future worlds,” say the artists. “In that sense, it helps us to rethink the past to envisage a better future.”BJP

Raquel Villar-Pérez is an independent curator, researcher and writer based in Edinburgh, UK. She is Associate Curator at the Women Photographers International Archive (WOPHA) and the inaugural Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Curatorial Fellow. She has previously held curatorial roles at Tate Modern, Photoworks, and Impressions Gallery. Her work has been supported by Arts Council England, Fundación Botín, and Art Fund, and she regularly serves as a juror and nominator for international photography awards, including the Hasselblad Award and the FOAM Paul Huf Award. She is currently pursuing a PhD at Edinburgh College of Art.

A witness statement from Russell Brand ’s former assistant has painted a picture of what it was like working for him in the noughties, as the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star’s rape and sexual assault trial enters its third week.

Russell Brand Trial: Witnesses Say Their Friend Was “Extremely Distressed” After Alleged Anal Rape

Russell Brand Told Woman “We Should Swap Numbers Now” After Alleged Oral Rape In Toilet

The PA, who worked for Brand during the decade that most of the alleged assaults took place, said he “loved walking around in his underwear with no shirt on,” had an “insane sexual appetite” and “never seemed happy after sex, more so depressed.”

Brand faces three charges of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of indecent assault based on allegations made by six women . His team will set out his defense later in the trial, and he denies all charges and has pleaded not guilty. Deadline has been reporting daily from a live video feed of the courtroom since the trial began.

Watch on Deadline

The assistant said she spent lots of time at Brand’s flat and was “exhausted emotionally” by the end as he was “a lot to deal with.”

She said he was incredibly busy at the time with presenting, media and comedy work and at the same time alleged his “insane sexual appetite” meant women were constantly coming over to his flat or dressing rooms. Once, the PA was told not to take Brand’s mum or girlfriend to his dressing room as he was having sex and “didn’t want them to see,” she alleged.

“At a certain point I realized he didn’t often know the women who were coming over,” read the statement. “He was like a peacock, women always approached him.”

While Brand was working and she was at his flat, the woman claimed Brand would “joke with me and say, ‘May I go and have sex now?’.” She added that he “never seemed happy after sex, more so depressed.”

The assistant stressed she “never witnessed Russell Brand doing anything against the law or didn’t have anyone disclose anything like that.”

She added: “I have worked with celebrities before and have seen a lot of people normalizing bad behavior, but this was on another level. Everyone normalizing Russell Brand’s behavior made me think, ‘I guess this is just the way it is here.'”

She said she stopped working with Brand eventually because she was “sick of him and feeling burnt out.”

Brand arrived once again at London’s Southwark Crown Court this morning with wife Laura Gallacher. The statement from his ex-assistant will be one of the final pieces of evidence in the prosecution’s case, with Brand’s defense expected to begin tomorrow and the actor expected to take the stand.

“He was a superstar”

Earlier, witness statements were read to the jury from people associated with a trio of Brand’s accusers.

One accuser has previously said she complained to Channel 4 about Brand’s behavior in 2009 after he allegedly put his head in her lap and demanded a massage.

The witness statement, which came from one of the complainant’s Channel 4 colleagues, said she was told that two of Brand’s associates ordered her to give him the massage several times, otherwise he would not record a radio advert. She said her colleague told her Brand’s associates “watched and laughed” while the alleged assault was taking place.

The jury was also read text messages from a different accuser, who said she was assaulted at a radio station , which argued why she didn’t report him at the time. “He was a superstar,” read the texts. “I thought nothing would happen to him.”

The sister of a different alleged victim, who said she was orally raped by Brand when attending the birthday party of a TV producer, provided a statement saying her sibling told her Brand’s eyes went “completely blank, and it was like he’d been possessed or was a completely different person” during the alleged attack.

The trial continues.

article_text:
Constantin Film and Sony Pictures’ horror reboot “ Resident Evil ” held onto first place at the mainland China box office during the Oct. 16–18 frame, pulling in RMB62.5 million ($9.3 million) in its second full weekend, according to data from Artisan Gateway.

Since rolling out in the late stretch of the Golden Week corridor on Oct. 5, the film has amassed a cumulative gross of $55.8 million.

Related Stories

‘The Altruists’ Trailer: Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner Star as Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison in Netflix Drama Series

New Classics Pictures’ crime procedural drama “ Traces of Justice ” maintained second position, grossing $6.8 million in its third weekend. Directed by Chen Sicheng (“Detective Chinatown”) and co-written with Zhang Ji and Yan Zijie, the period investigation epic has generated $84.6 million since its Oct. 1 release. Starring Zhang Yi, Ma Li, and Chen Minghao alongside guest appearances by Karry Wang, Fan Chengcheng, and Chen Feiyu, the multi-decade drama chronicles an elite public security detective unravelling major criminal mysteries based on real cases.

Beijing Joy Fun Pictures’ local body-swap comedy “Mr. & Mrs. Pardon” held third place, generating $4.1 million over the three-day weekend. Directed by Shen Chunyang and written by Ma Duo, the satirical feature starring real-life comedic duo Shen Chunyang and Xiao Shenyang alongside Jia Bing and Yu Yang has lifted its cume to $50.9 million since premiering on Oct. 1.

Popular on Variety

Dirty Monkeys’ war comedy-drama “ Once Upon a Time in the Middle East ” took fourth place in its tenth weekend, adding $900,000. Directed by Wen Muye and starring Shen Teng, Jiang Qiming, Aarif Rahman, and Omar Sherif, the enduring summer blockbuster has pushed its cumulative haul to $354.3 million since opening on Aug. 11, solidifying its place among the biggest commercial hits in the country this year.

Light Chaser Animation’s historical animated epic “Three Kingdoms: The Beginning” was in fifth spot, collecting $800,000 over the two-day weekend frame for a cumulative total of $14.7 million. Directed by Xie Junwei (“Chang’an”) and written by Wang Wei, the first installment in Light Chaser’s planned trilogy chronicles the political turmoil of the late Eastern Han dynasty and the battle for Luoyang, focusing on the intertwined ambitions of young warlords Cao Cao and Yuan Shao.

Mainland China’s overall weekend box office gross was $26.7 million amid an extended post-holiday slowdown. The 2026 year-to-date total stands at $4.67 billion, trailing the same period in 2025 by 29.2%.
