article_text:
Jamie Foxx has joined the indie crime thriller “East of the River” as a producer. He boards through his Foxxhole Productions alongside Alex Marks.

The film, directed by Dennis Latos, follows two estranged brothers reuniting to face the underground poker ring that destroyed their family. The film stars Ben Barnes (“The Chronicles of Narnia” franchise, “The Punisher”), Ben Ahlers (“The Gilded Age,” “Little Brother”), Callie Hernandez (“The Flight Attendant,” “Alien: Covenant”), Michael Abbott Jr. (“Verity,” “The Drama”) and Maria Sten in her first film role since starring in television’s “Neagley.”

Related Stories

'Children of Blood and Bone' Author Tomi Adeyemi Quietly Cancels New York Comic Con Panel

‘Blade Runner 2099’ Trailer: Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer Are Fugitives in Amazon Limited Series

The cast also includes David Zayas (“Dexter,” “Dexter: Resurrection”), John Bedford Lloyd (“Ozark”, “The Bourne Supremacy”), Catherine Curtin (“Stranger Things,” “Orange Is the New Black”), Nathan Wallace (“Daredevil: Born Again,” “NCIS: Origins”), and Steven Gregory (“Gravesend”). The film also features former WWE wrestler James Storm and former NFL running back Dalvin Cook.

Post-production of the film recently wrapped. Global distribution rights are available through CAA Media Finance.

“East of the River” was and written by Elise Finnerty with story by Jim Tamburino. Ben Grant served as director of photography on the film.

In addition to Foxx and Marks, the film is produced by Nicolas Alvo at Ruta 5 Films, and Benjamin Wiessner at Vanishing Angle, alongside Latos and Finnerty. Executive producers include David Schuster of Gloves Up Entertainment Steven Gregory, John Harms, Gerry Ambrose and Foxxhole Productions president Corinne Foxx. The film is presented by Gloves Up Entertainment in association with Echobend Pictures and The Dazey Phase.

“We’ve been fans of Dennis since first discovering his short film, ‘Leylak’, where his command of character and storytelling immediately stood out. This film is a powerful continuation of that voice, and we’re proud to support this exceptional project,” Jamie and Corrine Foxx and Marks said in a joint statement.

Latos said, “I wanted to capture the kinetic, dangerous energy of a world most people never see. This isn’t just a story about poker, it’s a high-octane look at what happens when you’re backed into a corner and forced to gamble with your life. We’ve fused a gritty family drama with the pulse-pounding stakes of the criminal underworld to give the audience a cinematic experience that is both deeply felt and truly thrilling.”

Schuster added, “When Dennis Latos and I set out to make our first independent feature film, I never imagined that we’d have such a talented cast and amazing crew. With Dennis and I originally being from Queens, this project is close to our hearts. I am grateful to our amazing producing partners, Jamie, Alex, Nicolas, Benjamin, and Elise.”

Barnes is represented by Gersh, Luber Roklin Entertainment and ID Public Relations. Ahlers is represented by Gersh, Artists First and Felker Toczek Suddleson McGinnis Ryan LLP. Hernandez is represented by Independent Artist Group, Entertainment 360 and Paul Hastings. Sten is represented by CAA, Brillstein Entertainment Partners, The Initiative Group and Granderson Des Rochers. Zayas is represented by Buchwald, ATA Management, Jill Fritzo Public Relations and Schreck Rose Dapello Adams Berlin & Dunham. Bedford Lloyd is represented by CESD Talent Agency. Curtin is represented by Artists & Representatives, Fusion Entertainment and Sullivan Talent Group. Wallace is represented by UIA Talent & Brian Twohig of Roger Paul Talent. Gregory is represented by Bright Artists Management.

article_text:
Five years ago, I would have been the last person you’d expect to care about a new “ Street Fighter ” movie. I had no real connection to the IP, only brief memories of playing the arcade game, and the quality of past films gave me no reason to suspect the franchise held cinematic stories waiting to be told. When Legendary, Capcom, and Paramount announced plans to reboot the franchise, my investment in the project never went beyond professional obligation.

And then the casting announcements began to roll in. Names like Noah Centineo, Andrew Koji, and even Jason Momoa seemed like straightforward choices for this kind of property. But as the ensemble cast around them began to take shape, each name left me more confused about what the film ‘s vision could possibly be. In Roman Reigns and Cody Rhodes, you had two of the biggest wrestlers in WWE — hardly the first wrestlers to try their hands at movie stardom, but neither has ever made a dent in Hollywood before. Andrew Schulz is a shock comedian firmly ensconced in the Joe Rogan and Kill Tony universes, while Eric Andre is an Adult Swim legend beloved on the opposite side of the alternative comedy spectrum. Then you add a gay music icon like Orville Peck and Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson playing a boxer, and you’re left with chaos.

As the film’s October 17 release date approached, “Street Fighter” was one of my most anticipated movies on the fall calendar. It was pure curiosity, as I couldn’t wrap my head around what an eclectic group of performers could possibly do on the same screen. (I thought “fighting” was a pretty safe bet based on the movie’s title, but there isn’t nearly as much as you might think!) The finished product is a mixed bag with high highs and low lows, but it’s never boring — largely because of the diversity and visible excitement of its cast.

It raises the question: Is meme casting Hollywood’s next great marketing strategy? Endless ink has been spilled about the decline of traditional movie stars and how casting the right celebrities no longer guarantees box office success. For the past decade, most of Hollywood has operated on the assumption that IP is the new movie star— if you have access to the right legacy character, the person wearing the costume is just an added bonus. But we’ve seen diminishing returns even for the most blue-chip IPs… when a new “Star Wars” movie loses to “Obsession” at the box office, you can tell moviegoers are itching for something new.

In a way, the new “Street Fighter” diverges from both strategies. It’s built around a recognizable IP, but the casting choices are so unique that you can’t help but walk in feeling like you’re going to see something new. You could compare the casting philosophy to a reverse “Expendables,” assembling the strangest possible group of faces that will polarize every audience member to some degree.

While the movie is set in 1993 (with prologues that stretch back to 1987), it does an exceptional job of capturing the absurd feeling of being alive in 2026. At times it almost feels like scrolling through an endless stream of ironic brand collabs with every celebrity under the sun (though the lighting is considerably better). Sometimes it feels like our very existence proves the old idea that postmodernism inevitably gives way to pastiche, and few films have capitalized on that better than “Street Fighter.”

Too many variables are at play to judge the entire “meme casting as marketing” strategy based on the success of “Street Fighter.” It’s still an IP people have preexisting relationships with (for better or worse), and mixed reviews will certainly factor into its success as well. But the film is currently tracking to open as high as $70 million globally this weekend — always an acceptable start for a film budgeted at $82 million. It’s fair to think that the bold casting choices are playing a large role in those numbers.

While we all search for novelty in an increasingly saturated media landscape, the prospect of seeing Orville Peck, 50 Cent, and David Dastmalchian walk into a bar in full anime garb might be even more intriguing to some viewers than watching a new film from Brad Pitt or Tom Cruise. That sentence would have sounded like insanity a few decades ago, but in the strange world of Hollywood in the 2020s, weirder might really be better.

A Paramount release, “Street Fighter” is now playing in theaters.
excerpt_original: Paramount's new "Street Fighter" reboot is generating as much hype for its eclectic cast as its IP. Its box-office success might be a case study in marketing through WTF casting.

article_text:
In a city like New York, what’s another film festival? When one can crop up in any neighborhood, keeping track is neither possible nor desirable. So if I might’ve accordingly raised an eyebrow to hear of the Downtown Festival upon its appearance in 2024, allow me a moment of judging a book by its cover.

Coming to know the festival and its founder, Rebekah Sherman-Myntti, has disavowed any wonky feelings. Downtown, now in its third year, is further and further proving itself a valuable companion to New York’s larger festivals: a repository for debut filmmakers, low-budget fare, or (speaking for myself and a small group of friends) an undistributed TV pilot that was shot in our apartments and serves as something of an all-male Girls riff. It’s a place that makes artists feel welcome and comfortable, allowing them to tailor a world premiere to their desires without excluding them from a larger flux.

Sherman-Myntti and I spoke about Downtown’s third year , which commences tonight with Paul Schrader’s The Basics of Philosophy , a film she says exemplifies the festival’s balance between legacy and discovery.

Let’s start with a basic question: can you tell me how the third edition of The Downtown Festival separates itself from predecessors?

I think this year feels quite a bit different. The first two editions were really about establishing the festival’s identity and proving the concept. In 2024, I wanted to see if this seemingly crazy idea could actually work and be pulled off. In 2025, it was really about realizing how much of an appetite there was for something like this to exist, which was super exciting. With the third edition this year, the scale is much bigger, the program is more ambitious, and the relationships between film, music, artist talks, and nightlife feel way more intertwined.

At the same time, the core idea of the festival hasn’t changed. It’s still artists-for-artists, deeply rooted in discovery, and focused on creating real exchanges between filmmakers, musicians, and various other disciplines. I’m always thinking about the kind of festival experience I’d genuinely want as a filmmaker… one where people feel supported, connected to their fellow artists as well as audiences, and part of something that can continue beyond a single event. We haven’t even announced half of our non-film programming yet! So stay tuned.

The Story of Eve by Alexandra Cabral

The program is impressive, albeit not comprising much that is even the least-bit known. I’m curious, also, about the distinction between programming a number of first-time filmmakers—exactly the kind of group that would struggle to be prioritized by programmers—and films that are plainly worthwhile, regardless of author. Do you see yourself prioritizing one while still hoping to serve another?

I definitely don’t prioritize first-time filmmakers just because they’re first-time filmmakers. I like to prioritize work that feels incredibly specific and like it has a real point of view. There has to be a certain aliveness to it. With films, we’re always looking for ones that feel deeply personal, where you can really sense that the filmmaker had to make this film in this way. Rather than something that could have been made by anyone or that feels like it’s trying to fit into an existing mold.

That said: I do feel really strongly about making space for artists who haven’t already been “validated” by the usual systems. If someone has made something amazing and doesn’t yet have representation, press, institutional support, or a recognizable name attached to them, that makes me more interested. I think festivals can play a meaningful role in helping people discover work they might not otherwise know about and in giving that work a context that helps audiences understand why it’s cool or important.

At the Downtown Festival, you can have a true legend like Paul Schrader showing work alongside a visual artist making her first feature, like Ondine Viñao, and have both works taken equally seriously. You can also have someone like Paul Tschinkel, whose work is so beautifully tied to an older New York art world and to documenting artists from that era, sitting alongside much newer and younger voices. I love those kinds of juxtapositions because they break down the hierarchy a bit. The work gets to speak for itself and our audience can experience someone they already know alongside someone they may be discovering for the very first time. That tension between legacy and discovery is super fascinating to me and it’s a huge part of what makes programming exciting and fun for me and Briana. There’s so much value in putting artists who helped shape a particular cultural moment in direct conversation with people who are reinterpreting or challenging it now.

How much do you see yourself as separate from the elite New York pack of ND/NF, Tribeca, and NYFF? Is there anything you actively seek to do differently?

I definitely see us as separate, but not in an antagonistic way. Those festivals have their own incredible histories, scales, and institutional roles. I really enjoy going to screenings at them. I would say that The Downtown Festival is something very different! The biggest differentiating factor is probably that we are truly multidisciplinary. Film is a huge part of it, but it exists alongside music, artist talks, performances, and other one-night-only events. I’m interested in what happens when all of those worlds actually overlap rather than being treated as separate cultural lanes. The festival is also very multigenerational and very explicitly artists-for-artists. I want somebody making their first film to feel as meaningfully included as somebody who has been making work for forty years. We’re much less interested in reinforcing traditional hierarchies around who is already considered “important” enough to deserve attention.

And structurally, we’re an extremely tiny team and we don’t have a huge institution or infrastructure behind us. That limitation has actually shaped the festival in a way I really value because it keeps things super personal and close to the artists. I also like the flexibility and organized chaos because with that comes the freedom of spontaneity! It’s great to have the independence to occasionally make decisions quickly or very last-minute and sometimes build programs around conversations and relationships rather than around a preexisting institutional framework or schedule.

With our film program, we’re interested not only in the film and the screening itself, but in everything that forms around it: who is in the room, who engages with the work, artists meeting each other, what conversations continue afterward, and what kinds of relationships or collaborations might emerge from that experience. For me, the festival is as much about creating the conditions for genuine artistic exchange as it is about presenting a slate of films.

It’s notable that this is not The Downtown Film Festival. You have a music showcase and events sponsored by MFNY. Do you see these as in any way linked to cinema? I won’t try to force some idea of “live concerts are actually cinema,” but there’s an interesting intersection of a communal vibe to screenings and actual communal events that aren’t screenings.

Very much so. The point was never to build a film festival that just happened to have a few side events. The multidisciplinary aspect is fundamental to what The Downtown Festival is, and for me, the connective tissue is the artists and the audience. Film, music, art, performance, and nightlife all create communal experiences in different ways, and I love what happens when those artists and audiences collide. Historically, downtown New York culture wasn’t neatly divided into disciplines. Filmmakers were hanging out with musicians, visual artists were acting in and making films, musicians were making movies, and everyone was ending up in the same clubs. There was a real fluidity to it.

I’m much more interested in that kind of cross-pollination than keeping everything professionally siloed, which I think happens far too often now. Especially in a festival context. I really don’t believe in “staying in your lane.” The festival is about creating a space where those different worlds can come together naturally. And a big shoutout to MFNY for supporting that vision this year!

Without asking you to give away too much, what do you see as an expansion in future years?

I’d love for The Downtown Festival to become a true home base for artists from around the world who are making work that doesn’t fit into established categories and who are looking for a genuine community around what they make. A huge part of that is continuing to bring different generations into direct conversation with one another. I want artists to be able to show work alongside people they might never otherwise be programmed with—for those combinations to create unexpected connections between the work, the artists, and our audience. I also want to expand the festival’s footprint across downtown New York, taking over more spaces and neighborhoods all throughout Lower Manhattan. Ultimately, I see the festival as part of a much larger artistic ecosystem. I’m also a filmmaker and producer working on a few projects that connect to that broader “Downtown” world. I can’t say too much yet but there’s more coming soon.

Do you prioritize anything in particular when programming short films and music videos? Or, say, a TV pilot?

Point of view above everything. With shorts especially, I’m very resistant to the idea that they’re simply calling cards or proof-of-concepts for features. A short should justify its own form, you know? It should feel like the artist chose that length because it was exactly the right container for the idea. With a TV pilot, I’m looking for the same thing: specificity, meaning, and whether the work creates a world I want to spend time in, or at least one that feels unmistakably its own. In the case of Fellas , you guys created a world that genuinely makes me laugh, but also has a lot of heart. I’m so excited for you to share it with our audience.

Fellas by Matthew Danger Lippman

The Roxy is an interesting space to hold a festival. As a single-screen theater, there’s a big bleed-through of the crowd for something that just ended and something that’s just beginning—you genuinely can’t tell who’s who. I fear I’m answering my own question, but can you tell me what you especially like about hosting a festival there?

They have been incredible hosts of The Downtown Festival’s film program! And after a few days, Roxy Cinema starts to feel like our little clubhouse—it’s the best. I love the setup and energy there because there’s so much natural crossover. People come out of one screening and run into someone arriving for the next, filmmakers stay for other films. Everyone ends up catching up in the lobby or green room. I’ve seen real deals get made and really awesome collaborations begin there. Remind me to tell you the story about Abel [Ferrara] yelling to Susan Seidelman’s husband from inside the cinema because he wanted to stay for Abel’s film but Susan had made a dinner reservation and they needed to leave ASAP. Hilarious.

Illyse Singer, the cinema’s director, has been incredibly, incredibly supportive of me on the filmmaking side of things as well as with the festival. I love her very much. The cinema’s projectionists Mitchell [Mailloux Glidden] and Dillon [Friend] really hold it down with all of the files (a massive undertaking) and the rest of the staff are amazing. It’s also just a beautiful place to watch a movie—like watching a film inside a jewel box. It’s a very intimate setting, which is different from some larger festivals where you’re in a massive theater watching a filmmaker speak on a stage that feels very far away—physically and emotionally!

Like any proper festival director, you have a great sense of style. What do you prioritize for Downtown fits?

[Laughs] That’s really nice of you. My go-to is sequins and leather pants—I basically spend the entire festival running around dressed like Michael Jackson.

The Downtown Festival is now underway.

article_text:
This article includes spoilers for You Can See Everything , a new documentary about Elizabeth Holmes now playing theatrically in the US.

Did it seem strange to you that Elizabeth Holmes’s X account remained so active after she reported to prison in 2023? You are not alone, and You Can See Everything , a new documentary about the businesswoman that was directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, may offer some reasons for the weirdness of her social media in the past few years.

As stated in the film, Holmes’s fiancé, Billy Evans, has been helping man her X account, which has opined on issues ranging from the assassination of Charlie Kirk to whether or not she is a fan of Taylor Swift. Evans claims in the documentary that he is merely posting messages sent to him by Holmes from prison, where she still has email access.

But might he be putting words in her mouth and writing her posts for her? The film repeatedly raises that possibility, suggesting that Holmes may have lost control of her image while she remains incarcerated. (Her X posts are accompanied by her initials when she has actually written them, one post from September noted. “Posts without that signature are from the team managing this account,” that post continued.)

These questions have led many to revisit her X account, which includes a bizarre art connection in the form of her background: an image of Norman Rockwell ‘s 1943 painting Freedom of Speech , in which a man stands up and prepares to speak before a crowd. Rockwell made the painting in response to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s 1941 State of the Union address, wherein he called the right to freedom of speech an essential one. The painting is these days best known as a meme image used alongside an unpopular opinion.

Except that in Holmes’s version, Holmes herself stands in place of the man, wearing her signature black turtleneck. Roosevelt’s painting looks like it has been edited digitally, perhaps using an AI generator. In light of You Can See Everything , it’s an unsettling image: Holmes is unable to entirely speak for herself, even though her X account suggests otherwise.

“There is never a perfect moment worth waiting for,” reads one X from the account that featured the full version of the Rockwell-inspired image. “You have to take every step, every action you can – especially in the worst of circumstances – to fight for every fraction of an inch forward.”

It’s not the only art-related post her account has made. There’s also one featuring Michelangelo ‘s Pietà, along with a note that a book about the artist by Otto Mower.

“Last night I read an overview of Michaelangelo’s life by Otto Mower, a teacher who has very special meaning in our lives,” that post from September 2025 notes, misspelling the artist’s name. “He writes ‘for Michaelangelo, God was perfection. He felt that whoever strives for perfection is striving for the divine.’ Strive for the divine.”

That post notably does not have Holmes’s initials appended to it.

Neither does a post from April of this year that featured an image of Rembrandt’s 1633 painting The Storm on the Sea of Galilee , which was stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner museum in 1990 and has yet to be recovered. “Today is a storm on all the fronts, and so I rise through every wave,” the post says.

article_text:
‘D on’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a young Val Kilmer , not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant.

Not just yet, judging by the extended glimpse of the film released earlier this year : it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger.

Many reacted with revulsion to last year’s unveiling of AI “starlet” Tilly Norwood . After her appearance in an introductory “comedy” sketch, Emily Blunt described her as “really, really scary” – underscoring the depth of feeling around the idea of synthetic performers supplanting real ones. What you might call the Norwood injunction – the feeling of a tech-driven agenda imposing something no one asked for – deepened with the announcement the AI-lister will be soon appear in feature-length film Misaligned .

Tim Webber, the chief creative officer at British VFX powerhouse Framestore, is sceptical about whether fully AI-generated actors can ever capture the complexity of our inner lives. “AI models are trained on the surface of things – the pixels of internet images, if they’re image models. To get to the level where it’s a human performance, where there’s genuine emotion involved, is a long way further down,” he says. So AI acting, scraping the external texture of past performances, would seem to be the inverse of something like method acting – whose acolytes excavate their internal psyche and emotions in the interests of authenticity.

But AI acting is undeniably becoming more realistic. Higgsfield AI – one of many companies currently pushing the possibilities of AI video – recently claimed to have “eliminated” the uncanny valley: that nagging phoneysimilitude effect that has plagued even sophisticated recent CGI reincarnations, such as the de-aged Indiana Jones in The Dial of Destiny .

Having released two full-length, entirely AI-generated features this year, Higgsfield’s content lead Adil Alimzhanov is bullish. This new frontier of completely AI-generated films is liberating for artists, he says, and shortcuts laborious Hollywood production structures. The two online-only releases – Hell Grind , a 95-minute action fantasy, and The Cully Hill Boys, a 115-minute Guy Ritchie-esque caper comedy – completed the equivalent of shooting and post-production in a fortnight and a month respectively (not counting time spent on the scripts). Despite actors’ qualms, the future can’t be resisted, says Alimzhanov, 23, who used his own face for Hell Grind’s protagonist. “We can’t fight new tools simply because they transform industries. If you draw a parallel with when cars first came out, if we’d fought that, everybody would still be riding horses today.”

Hell Grind and The Cully Hill Boys are essentially extended ads for Higgsfield’s suite of AI content-creation tools. But they show swift progression on the AI acting front. In Hell Grind, released in May, the skate-rat characters only seem to be able to crank out a single emotion per 15-second shot (the limit of the Chinese video-AI model used, Seedance 2.0). The Cully Hill Boys, which came out three months later, is far more engaging, with enough convincing repartee and comic timing to qualify it as quite funny. Its lead trio of grime rappers on the lam are AI-generated likenesses of real-life streetball player Matt Kiatipis, MMA fighter Israel Adesanya and livestreamer N3on – testament to the gen Z, AI-native short-form creators Higgsfield aims to attract. Though there is something quaint about the idea of an “actor” in the age of AI. If bespoke characters can be generated for every film, why have an intermediary play a “role”?

Written by a human being, Tim Planagan, The Cully Hill Boys was assembled in 30-second chunks, made possible by this summer’s release of Seedance 2.5. But prompting your way towards something dramatically convincing is labour-intensive. First, visual “assets” are created of the characters – detailed body-length shots and facial closeups that are used to establish continuity when fed into video-generation prompts. Then, using the assets as an anchor point, each 30-second segment is defined in a 4,000-word prompt (itself partly generated by an LLM) defining the key parameters: action, camera movement, lighting and, of course, the emotions on display. The prompts are revised and the scene regenerated until the uncanny valley is hopefully bridged.

Where, say, Klaus Kinski could summon torrents of rage by tapping into his personal demons, an AI programmer has to achieve the same effect in much more approximate ways. “An AI is not an actor, so how do you communicate the internal state of a character?” says Zack London, who as Gossip Goblin makes highly baroque AI-generated sci-fi shorts. “You can say: they look confused, or they say this in jest, or they say this sternly. But it’s such a broad stroke. The model will probably come out with a very over-the-top telenovela-type performance, or will just not understand.” At that point, it becomes a case of treating the model like a “marionette doll” and tweaking individual strings. “You could say: there’s a slight quiver on the left side of their lip, and then their gaze diverts slightly downwards, and they look up again and blink.”

London chooses to keep a human ghost in the machine by first recording dialogue with real actors, around which he retro-fits the animation. He is candid about the shortcomings of the current prompting process, saying the results suit a certain type of film: “The acting is not going to be particularly subtle, like some grand Anthony Hopkins or Olivia Colman performance. It’s more like an old-school Terry Gilliam or Guy Ritchie performance, where the characters are larger than life.” But maybe that’s where the danger lies for actors: many blockbuster performances, meting out simple beats of easily comprehensible emotion, have a cut-and-paste quality – and are therefore susceptible to AI.

Then again, a mundane magic still happens even on blockbuster sets. “Sometimes the most brilliant moment happens in the fraction of a second. And you can’t put your finger on why an actor gives a certain look,” says Tye Sheridan , the co-founder (in 2016) of Wonder Dynamics, an Autodesk company who developed the AI production tool Autodesk Flow Studio. He should know: he was the star of Steven Spielberg’s 2018 film Ready Player One , which itself patrolled the frontier between real and digital.

Sheridan shares Higgsfield’s belief that AI-driven methods can democratise film-making. But he is adamant that performances should retain a human core. Flow Studio uses AI for an augmented and far cheaper version of motion capture, layering CG characters and environments on top of filmed footage. At Framestore, Webber is exploring similar AI tools that allow him to apply what he calls “digital makeup” to traditional performances, without the guesswork involved in generative prompts.

He, London and Sheridan agree that this hybrid form of film-making still allows actors to make specific choices essential to authentic creation. “You have to ask, with these generative models: are they really designed to deliver legendary performances, or are they designed to cut to an average?” asks Sheridan. Alimzhanov, though, insists something akin to an actor’s internal process is achievable via AI. The prompting used on The Cully Hill Boys was different in one key regard: instead of replicating emotions by specifying the physical mechanics, the AI model generated sequences based on contextual input about what the characters were experiencing.

These two camps of AI acting – technological and human-centric – are fighting the latest bout in the struggle between the forces that have shaped the craft: external v internal; reproducing v experiencing; Laurence Olivier telling Dustin Hoffman that, instead of staying awake for 72 hours, he should “try acting, dear boy”. But where Stanislavsky promoted the internal quest to revitalise acting, this could be the first time in the modern era when the formalist approach – the mannered reproduction of emotions – looks like the future.

Opening the digital floodgates could lead to William Gibson territory , where deathless virtual stars seduce the masses, as in his 1996 novel Idoru. But it’s still not clear whether the box office demand, and thus a true economic case, for AI cinema exists. And we’re yet to see a compelling script that crystallises the possibilities of the tech in story form, as The Matrix did for CGI. If we’re inundated with unloved AI abominations, the words of Val Kilmer in Tombstone, playing that icon of human mortality, Doc Holliday, will ring anew: “There’s just something about him. Something around the eyes reminds me of … me. I’m sure of it – I hate him.”

Isabelle Kalandar, who both directed and produced “Another Birth,” received the Cultural Diversity Award for the Tajikistan, U.S. and Qatar collaboration. India’s R. Gowtham earned the Young Cinema Award, given with NETPAC, for “Members of the Problematic Family.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Malaysian filmmaker Haziqah Azemi won the Forum Filmmaker Award, run with The Post Lounge Group, for her project “Garek.” The story centers on a woman whose relationship is tested when she faces religious persecution after becoming pregnant outside marriage. article_text:
Georgian filmmaker Levan Koguashvili’s “Guria” was named best film at the 19th Asia Pacific Screen Awards , handed out Oct. 30 at The Star Gold Coast in Queensland, Australia.

Koguashvili shared the prize with fellow producers Olena Yershova and Boris Frumin. The film was made across seven countries: Georgia, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Bulgaria, Türkiye, Norway and Saudi Arabia.

Related Stories

Elizabeth Holmes Mania: 'You Can See Everything' Drives 186% Viewership Spike for Amanda Seyfried's 'The Dropout' (EXCLUSIVE)

'You Can See Everything': That Shocking, Meta Twist With [SPOILER] Explained in Elizabeth Holmes Doc

Thai director Sompot Chidgasornpongse won best director for “9 Temples to Heaven,” a co-production involving Thailand, Singapore, France, Norway, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia and Qatar. Myanmar’s Aung Phyoe received a special mention in the directing category for “Fruit Gathering.” Afghan director Shahrbanoo Sadat took the Jury Grand Prize for “No Good Men.”

This year’s field comprised 36 nominated films from 32 countries and regions.

Nepalese actor Pushpa Thing Lama won best performance for “Elephants in the Fog,” and South Korea’s Sim Su-bin was named best new performer for “The World Before.” The screenplay award went to Rakan Mayasi, Wahid Ajmi and Pôl Seif for “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep,” backed by Belgium, Lebanon, Palestine, Qatar and Saudi Arabia. Vietnamese cinematographer Nguyễn Vinh Phúc won for “Hearing.”

New Zealand’s Paloma Schneideman took best youth film for “Big Girls Don’t Cry,” produced by Vicky Pope and Thomas Coppell. The animation prize went to “The Violinist,” a co-production between Singapore, Spain and Italy that was co-directed by Singapore’s Ervin Han and Spain’s Raúl García.

Itab Azzam and Jack MacInness won best documentary for “One in a Million,” a U.K.-U.S. film that follows the life of a Syrian refugee. Isabelle Kalandar, who both directed and produced “Another Birth,” received the Cultural Diversity Award for the Tajikistan, U.S. and Qatar collaboration. India’s R. Gowtham earned the Young Cinema Award, given with NETPAC, for “Members of the Problematic Family.”

Malaysian filmmaker Haziqah Azemi won the Forum Filmmaker Award, run with The Post Lounge Group, for her project “Garek.” The story centers on a woman whose relationship is tested when she faces religious persecution after becoming pregnant outside marriage. Azemi, who took part in the Griffith Film School and APSA Regional Reels program, came back to APSA this year after developing the project with mentoring from APSA Academy member Yulia Evina Bhara.

Tracey Vieira, chair of the Asia Pacific Screen Awards, said: “From ‘Guria’ and ‘No Good Men’ to ‘Elephants in the Fog,’ this year’s winners remind us of the extraordinary stories emerging from our region and the importance of creating opportunities for these voices to be recognized internationally.”

Veteran Indian producer Bobby Bedi was handed the FIAPF Award for outstanding contribution to film in the Asia Pacific. Luis Alberto Scalella, president of FIAPF, said: “Through landmark films such as ‘Bandit Queen’ and ‘Fire,’ he has championed powerful stories that have challenged audiences and resonated far beyond India.”

The ceremony also revealed five projects selected for the 2026 MPA APSA Academy Film Fund, each of which will get a $10,000 grant funded entirely by the Motion Picture Association. They are Payal Kapadia’s “A Memory of Being Here” (India), produced by Thomas Hakim; Davy Chou’s “My Father’s Glory” (France, Cambodia), produced by Charlotte Vincent; Taifeng Liu’s “A Place in the Sun” (China), produced by Janet (Yan Yan) Wu; Nicole Midori Woodford’s “Incarnation” (Singapore, Japan), produced by Anthony Chen; and Zhanana Kurmasheva’s documentary “The Story of My Shirt” (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, China, Chile), produced by Banu Ramazanova.

Three of the five projects are directed by women. Chen returns to the fund after working on “We Are All Strangers,” which received a grant in 2023 and was among this year’s nominees.

Urmila Venugopalan, president and managing director, Asia Pacific, at the Motion Picture Association, said the success of films such as “9 Temples to Heaven,” which received MPA APSA Academy Film Fund support in 2021, “shows the importance of supporting filmmakers and their stories from the earliest stages of development.”

Every APSA nominee, along with members of the nominations councils and juries, joins the APSA Academy, whose president is Australian screen veteran Jack Thompson. The body now has upward of 1,816 members across 84 countries and areas.

The full list of winners:

Best Director – Special Mention Aung Phyoe, “Fruit Gathering” (Myanmar, Czech Republic, France)

Best Youth Film “Big Girls Don’t Cry,” dir. Paloma Schneideman; prod. Vicky Pope, Thomas Coppell (New Zealand)

Best Animated Film “The Violinist,” dir. Ervin Han, Raúl García; prod. Paloma Mora, Cristiano Bortone, Justin Deimen, Leonard Lai, Takafumi Yuki (Singapore, Spain, Italy)

Best Documentary Film “One in a Million,” dir. Itab Azzam, Jack MacInness; prod. Itab Azzam, Jack MacInness, Will Anderson, James Bluemel, Andrew Palmer, Raney Aronson-Rath (U.K., U.S.)

Best Screenplay Rakan Mayasi, Wahid Ajmi, Pôl Seif, “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep” (Belgium, Lebanon, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia)

Best Cinematography Nguyễn Vinh Phúc, “Hearing” (Vietnam, Singapore, Norway, France, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, Cambodia, Thailand, Taiwan)

Best Performance Pushpa Thing Lama, “Elephants in the Fog” (Nepal, Germany, Brazil, France, Norway)

Best New Performer Sim Su-bin, “The World Before” (South Korea)

Cultural Diversity Award “Another Birth,” dir./prod. Isabelle Kalandar (Tajikistan, U.S., Qatar)

Young Cinema Award (in partnership with Netpac) R. Gowtham, “Members of the Problematic Family” (India)

FIAPF Award Bobby Bedi (India)

Forum Filmmaker Award Haziqah Azemi, “Garek” (Malaysia)

article_text:
Bridge Independent has boarded psychological horror film “Henry’s Ebb,” which stars Kingston Rumi Southwick , one of the stars of “Widow’s Bay.” The film makes its world premiere at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival .

“Henry’s Ebb,” written and directed by Thomas Mendolia in his feature debut, also stars Banks Repeta (“The Black Phone”), Ashley Shelton and Will Holland, with supporting performances from Rebecca Koon and Austin Willard.

Related Stories

DJ Pikachu: Pokémon Goes EDM With Lasers, Battles and Marshmello in 30th Anniversary Concert at Intuit Dome

Nathan Fielder Negotiated a ‘Kill Switch’ on ‘You Can See Everything,’ Says Lance Oppenheim: ‘If We Didn’t Find Something, We Could Just Throw It All Away’

The film follows Henry, a boy who flees his troubled home in search of the father he barely remembers, accompanied by Ebb, the imaginary friend Henry created to help him survive a tumultuous childhood. But as their journey leads them through the backroads of the American South, Ebb’s protection becomes increasingly controlling, forcing Henry to question the companion he has always trusted.

Popular on Variety

Bill Straus of Bridge Independent is handling domestic sales, with Logan Taylor of New Ratio Films serving as sales and distribution consultant.

The film is produced by Ford Films’ Lucas Ford and Joey LePage, with Tony Tehle and Irina Slepneva serving as co-producers.

“Henry’s Ebb” was previously selected for the Frontières Buyers Showcase at the Marché du Film during the Cannes Film Festival.

The film will have its U.S. premiere at Cucalorus Film Festival in North Carolina, where the production was filmed and set.

In a statement, Mendolia spoke about Elkin, North Carolina, the town in which he grew up and where he shot the film: “Elkin exists in my mind as both magical and painful, and that duality felt essential to the story. I wrote it around real locations from my memory, and knew that shooting here was crucial. Henry moves through a world that is full of wonder, but also shaped by the complicated lives of the adults around him. Setting the film there allowed those two feelings to coexist in the same space.”

article_text:
Editor’s Note: This story originally appeared in On Balance , the ARTnews newsletter about the art market and beyond. Sign up here to receive it every Wednesday.

Happy Wednesday! Here’s a round-up of who’s moving and shaking in the art trade this week.

Vielmetter Los Angeles Takes On Painter Patrick Eugène: The Brooklyn-born, Atlanta-based artist, whose figurative work draws on his Haitian heritage, will debut with the gallery at Art Basel Miami Beach in December ahead of a solo exhibition in Los Angeles in fall 2027.

Ruiz-Healy Art Announces Representation of the Mel Casas Estate: The San Antonio– and New York–based gallery has taken on exclusive representation of 50 percent of the Chicano painter’s estate (1929–2014), in partnership with three of his children. Solo exhibitions at both locations are planned for 2027.

Qatar Museums Names Azu Nwagbogu Artistic Director of Tasweer 2027: The writer and curator is a founder of the LagosPhoto Biennale and the founder and director of the Lagos-based non-profit art space African Artists’ Foundation. He will lead the fourth edition of the Doha-based photography biennial.

John Michael Kohler Arts Center and Kohler Co. Announce 2027 Arts/Industry Residency Artists: The 2027 artists-in-residence are Emily Endo, Raul De Lara, Amy Yoes, Erin Jane Nelson, Esther Elia, Christina Forrer, Jiha Moon, Tyanna Buie, Ben Gould, Gina Michaels, Chenlu Hou, and Jude Griebel.

The Big Number: $100 M.+

That’s the approximate asking price for Amedeo Modigliani ‘s 1917 painting Nu étendu (Lolotte) , on offer from Pace Di Donna Schrader at Art Basel Paris—which would make it by far the most expensive work reported at the fair so far. The painting was featured in Modigliani’s only solo exhibition during his lifetime, at Galerie Berthe Weill in 1917, and then purchased from the artist’s dealer in 1920 by the family of its present owner. The presentation marks the work’s return to the market after roughly a century. And it’s just the latest Modigliani to reach the market: last week, Phillips announced it would offer a rare limestone sculpture by the artist at its New York sales in November, carrying a $35 million estimate. Modigliani momentum is clearly in the air.

Read This

Jeff Koons , who can sometimes seem to operate on a wavelength all his own, delivered once more last week on the Middlebrow Podcast , whose latest episode is a wide-ranging interview touching on everything from his early-career job at the Museum of Modern Art to his sprawling studio. Which younger artists are making notable work, in Koons’s opinion? “Jordan Wolfson, here in New York, is making great work,” he says. (A natural response, given that the two are both represented by Gagosian, where Wolfson is showing an AI-generated take on a painting from Koons’s “Made in Heaven” series.) Is AI useful for generating ideas? “I wouldn’t have confidence in AI for that at this time,” Koons says. The best architectural project of the past two and a half decades? “I’ve never been to Vegas. I only want to go for the Sphere—I think it’s the most exciting building of the 21st century.” Sure! — Alex Greenberger, Deputy Editor
